topics.summary: How protons, neutrons and electrons are arranged in an atom, and how the four quantum numbers fix where each electron sits. Electron configurations underlie periodicity, bonding and spectra, so NSMQ uses this topic constantly for quick-fire configuration, quantum-number and spectral-line questions.
keyIdeas: Atomic number Z = number of protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A and almost identical chemistry.
Principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, …; azimuthal l = 0 to n − 1 (s, p, d, f for l = 0, 1, 2, 3); magnetic mₗ = −l to +l; spin mₛ = +½ or −½.
Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.
Aufbau principle: subshells fill in order of increasing (n + l); when two subshells tie, the one with lower n fills first.
Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing, e.g. N 2p³ has three unpaired electrons.
Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ because half-filled and filled d subshells are extra stable.
Transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d when they form ions: Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶, not [Ar]3d⁴4s².
Hydrogen emission series: Lyman ends at n = 1 (ultraviolet), Balmer at n = 2 (visible), Paschen at n = 3 (infrared).

formulas.name: Mass number
formulas.note: N = number of neutrons. Neutrons = A − Z.

formulas.name: Relative atomic mass
formulas.note: Weighted average over all isotopes; why Cl is 35.5, not a whole number.

formulas.name: Orbitals in a shell and subshell
formulas.formula: shell: n² orbitals; subshell: 2l + 1 orbitals holding 2(2l + 1) electrons
formulas.note: s, p, d, f have 1, 3, 5, 7 orbitals and 2, 6, 10, 14 electrons.

formulas.name: Nodes in an orbital
formulas.formula: total nodes = n − 1; angular nodes = l; radial nodes = n − l − 1
formulas.note: 3p: 2 nodes in total, 1 angular and 1 radial.

formulas.name: Bohr energy levels
formulas.note: For hydrogen (Z = 1) and hydrogen-like ions such as He⁺ and Li²⁺ only. 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

formulas.name: Rydberg equation
formulas.note: R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹; n₂ > n₁; n₁ is the lower level the electron falls to.

formulas.name: de Broglie wavelength
formulas.note: Wave nature of electrons; heavier or faster particles have shorter wavelengths.

formulas.name: Number of spectral lines
formulas.note: All possible lines when electrons fall from level n down to n = 1 in a sample of atoms.

formulas.name: Spin-only magnetic moment
formulas.note: u = number of unpaired electrons; u = 0 means diamagnetic.

shortcuts.name: (n + l) filling rule
shortcuts.rule: Add n + l for each subshell; smaller sum fills first; on a tie, smaller n first.
shortcuts.example: 6s: 6 + 0 = 6; 4f: 4 + 3 = 7; 5d: 5 + 2 = 7. So the order is 6s, then 4f (n = 4 smaller), then 5d.

shortcuts.name: Spectral lines count
shortcuts.rule: Lines from level n = n(n − 1)/2, i.e. the triangular number of (n − 1).
shortcuts.example: Electrons excited to n = 5: 5 × 4/2 = 10 lines. From n = 4: 4 × 3/2 = 6 lines.

shortcuts.name: Noble-gas core then remove 4s first
shortcuts.rule: Subtract the previous noble gas's Z, fill 4s then 3d; for cations strip 4s before 3d.
shortcuts.example: Fe, Z = 26: 26 − 18 = 8 → [Ar]4s²3d⁶. Fe³⁺: remove 4s² and one 3d → [Ar]3d⁵, five unpaired electrons.

shortcuts.name: Hydrogen-like ionisation energy
shortcuts.rule: Ionisation energy from the ground state = 13.6 × Z² eV.

shortcuts.name: Two-isotope average
shortcuts.rule: Start from the lighter mass and add (abundance of heavier isotope × mass difference).

traps: Writing quantum numbers with l = n (for example a '2d' orbital): l can only go up to n − 1, so 1p, 2d and 3f do not exist.
Removing 3d electrons before 4s when writing transition-metal ions: Cu²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁹, not [Ar]3d⁸4s¹.
Forgetting the Cr and Cu exceptions and writing 3d⁴4s² or 3d⁹4s².
Confusing mass number (a whole number for one isotope) with relative atomic mass (a weighted average).
Pairing electrons too early: O 2p⁴ has two unpaired electrons, not zero.
nsmqTips: For 'how many unpaired electrons' questions, write only the outer subshell and draw boxes in your head; for d⁵ the answer is 5, for d⁶ and d⁴ it is 4.
Quantum-number sets: check l < n first, then |mₗ| ≤ l, then mₛ = ±½. Most 'which set is not allowed' options fail on the first test.
Learn the H series names and regions as a triple (Lyman–UV–n=1, Balmer–visible–n=2, Paschen–IR–n=3); these are asked as quick recall.

topics.summary: The mole links the mass, number of particles, gas volume and concentration of a substance, and balanced equations give the mole ratios between reactants and products. Nearly every numerical chemistry question in NSMQ passes through a mole calculation, so speed here pays off everywhere.
keyIdeas: One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant, N_A).
Molar mass in g mol⁻¹ equals the relative formula mass Mᵣ.
Coefficients in a balanced equation are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of moles (Avogadro's law), so gas volume ratios equal mole ratios.
The limiting reagent is used up first and fixes the maximum amount of product.
Empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it.
Concentration in mol dm⁻³ is moles per dm³ of solution; 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.

formulas.name: Moles from mass
formulas.note: m in g, M in g mol⁻¹.

formulas.name: Moles from particles
formulas.note: N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

formulas.name: Moles of gas
formulas.note: V_m = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ at s.t.p. (0 °C, 1 atm); about 24 dm³ mol⁻¹ at room conditions.

formulas.name: Molar concentration
formulas.note: V in dm³; convert cm³ by dividing by 1000.

formulas.name: Mass concentration
formulas.note: Converts mol dm⁻³ into g dm⁻³.

formulas.name: Dilution
formulas.note: Moles of solute stay the same when only water is added.

formulas.name: Titration ratio
formulas.note: a and b are the coefficients of A and B in the balanced equation.

formulas.name: Percentage by mass of an element
formulas.note: For example % N in NH₄NO₃ = 28/80 × 100 = 35%.

formulas.name: Percentage yield
formulas.note: Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent.

formulas.name: Molecular formula
formulas.formula: molecular formula = (Mᵣ / empirical formula mass) × empirical formula
formulas.note: The multiplier must be a whole number.

formulas.name: Atom economy
formulas.formula: atom economy = (M of desired product / total M of reactants) × 100
formulas.note: Uses the balanced equation; measures waste, not yield.

formulas.name: Hydrocarbon combustion
formulas.formula: CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4) O₂ → x CO₂ + (y/2) H₂O
formulas.note: Gives oxygen demand directly.

shortcuts.name: Assume 100 g
shortcuts.rule: For percentage composition, treat the percentages as grams, divide by Aᵣ, then divide by the smallest.

shortcuts.name: Oxygen demand of a hydrocarbon
shortcuts.rule: Moles of O₂ per mole of CₓHᵧ = x + y/4.
shortcuts.example: C₃H₈: 3 + 8/4 = 5 mol O₂. C₂H₄: 2 + 1 = 3 mol O₂.

shortcuts.name: Gas volumes as mole ratios
shortcuts.rule: For gases at the same T and P, read volumes straight from the coefficients.
shortcuts.example: 20 cm³ CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: needs 40 cm³ O₂ and gives 20 cm³ CO₂.

shortcuts.name: One-line titration
shortcuts.rule: c_unknown = (ratio) × c_known × V_known / V_unknown.
shortcuts.example: 25.0 cm³ NaOH needs 12.5 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ (2 NaOH : 1 H₂SO₄): c = 2 × 0.10 × 12.5/25.0 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.

shortcuts.name: Divide by coefficient for limiting reagent
shortcuts.rule: Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient; the smallest result is limiting.
shortcuts.example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O with 4 g H₂ (2 mol ÷ 2 = 1) and 64 g O₂ (2 mol ÷ 1 = 2): H₂ is limiting, so 2 mol H₂O = 36 g.

shortcuts.name: Half-mole water
shortcuts.rule: Know that 9 g of water is 0.5 mol, then scale.
shortcuts.example: 9 g H₂O = 0.5 mol = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules; each has 3 atoms, so 9.03 × 10²³ atoms.

traps: Using mass ratios from the equation instead of mole ratios.
Forgetting to convert cm³ to dm³ (divide by 1000) before using c = n/V.
Using single atoms for diatomic gases: 32 g of oxygen gas is 1 mol O₂, not 2 mol.
Leaving out water of crystallisation: CuSO₄·5H₂O has M = 249.5 g mol⁻¹, not 159.5 g mol⁻¹.
Using 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ when the question states room temperature (use about 24 dm³ mol⁻¹).
nsmqTips: Memorise common molar masses: H₂O 18, CO₂ 44, NaOH 40, HCl 36.5, H₂SO₄ 98, CaCO₃ 100, NaCl 58.5, Na₂CO₃ 106. Skipping the addition saves seconds.
In riddles that give a gas volume at s.t.p., divide by 22.4 first; 11.2 dm³ is 0.5 mol and 5.6 dm³ is 0.25 mol.
State the answer with its unit (mol, g, mol dm⁻³); quizmasters can reject a bare number.

topics.topic: States of matter and gas laws
topics.summary: This topic covers how particle motion and intermolecular forces give solids, liquids and gases their properties, and how gas pressure, volume, temperature and amount are related. NSMQ favours quick gas-law ratio questions, Graham's law and kinetic-theory recall.
keyIdeas: Kinetic theory of an ideal gas: particles of negligible volume move randomly, collide elastically and have no intermolecular forces; average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature.
Real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, and for polar or large molecules (NH₃, H₂O, CO₂ more than He, H₂).
Compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT); Z = 1 for an ideal gas.
All gas-law calculations need temperature in kelvin: T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.
A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, so water boils below 100 °C at high altitude.
The triple point is where solid, liquid and vapour coexist; above the critical temperature a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
Diffusion and effusion rates are inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass.

formulas.name: Boyle's law
formulas.note: Fixed n and T.

formulas.name: Charles's law
formulas.note: Fixed n and P; T in K.

formulas.name: Pressure law (Gay-Lussac)
formulas.note: Fixed n and V; T in K.

formulas.name: Combined gas law
formulas.note: Fixed amount of gas.

formulas.name: Ideal gas equation
formulas.note: R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (P in Pa, V in m³) or 0.0821 dm³ atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

formulas.name: Molar mass from density
formulas.note: Rearranged ideal gas equation; ρ in g dm⁻³ gives M in g mol⁻¹ with R = 0.0821 and P in atm.

formulas.name: Dalton's law of partial pressures
formulas.formula: P_total = P₁ + P₂ + …; Pᵢ = xᵢ P_total
formulas.note: xᵢ = mole fraction of gas i.

formulas.name: Graham's law
formulas.note: Rate of effusion or diffusion; time taken is proportional to √M.

formulas.name: Kinetic gas equation
formulas.note: c̄² = mean square speed; N = number of molecules of mass m.

formulas.name: Average kinetic energy
formulas.note: Depends only on temperature, not on the identity of the gas.

formulas.name: Root-mean-square speed
formulas.note: M in kg mol⁻¹.

formulas.name: van der Waals equation
formulas.note: a corrects for attractions, b for molecular volume.

shortcuts.name: Graham ratio by inspection
shortcuts.rule: Take the square root of the molar-mass ratio, heavier over lighter; the lighter gas is that many times faster.
shortcuts.example: H₂ (2) vs O₂ (32): √16 = 4, H₂ is 4 times faster. CH₄ (16) vs SO₂ (64): √4 = 2.

shortcuts.name: Unknown molar mass from effusion time
shortcuts.rule: If gas X takes k times as long as a reference gas, M_X = k² × M_ref.
shortcuts.example: X takes twice as long as O₂: M_X = 4 × 32 = 128 g mol⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Molar mass from density at s.t.p.
shortcuts.example: ρ = 1.25 g dm⁻³: M = 1.25 × 22.4 = 28 g mol⁻¹ (N₂ or CO).

shortcuts.name: Vapour density doubling
shortcuts.rule: Mᵣ = 2 × vapour density (vapour density is relative to H₂).
shortcuts.example: Vapour density 22 → Mᵣ = 44 (CO₂ or C₃H₈).

shortcuts.name: Gas law by multiplying ratios
shortcuts.rule: Start with the old value and multiply by a ratio for each change, choosing each ratio so it moves the value the right way.

shortcuts.name: rms speed scaling
shortcuts.rule: c_rms ∝ √T: quadrupling T (in K) doubles the speed; doubling T multiplies it by about 1.41.
shortcuts.example: 300 K → 1200 K: speed doubles. 300 K → 600 K: speed × 1.41.

traps: Using degrees Celsius in gas laws: doubling from 20 °C to 40 °C does not double the volume (293 K → 313 K).
Thinking heavier gas molecules have more kinetic energy at the same temperature; they have the same Eₖ and simply move more slowly.
Mixing units of R: 8.314 needs Pa and m³; 0.0821 needs atm and dm³.
Saying real gases behave ideally at high pressure; it is the opposite.
Treating rate and time in Graham's law the same way: rate ∝ 1/√M but time ∝ √M.
nsmqTips: Most gas-law riddles can be done with the multiply-by-ratios method without writing an equation; sense-check that heating expands and compressing raises pressure.
Expect 'which gas diffuses fastest' with a list; pick the smallest molar mass.
Know the ideal-gas assumptions as a list; a recall round may ask you to give two.

topics.summary: Energetics measures the heat taken in or given out by reactions and uses Hess's law, bond enthalpies and Born–Haber cycles to find enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly. Entropy and Gibbs energy then show whether a reaction is feasible, which NSMQ tests with sign reasoning and short calculations.
keyIdeas: Exothermic reactions have ΔH < 0 (heat released, surroundings warm); endothermic reactions have ΔH > 0.
Standard conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa (1 bar, often taken as 1 atm), 1 mol dm⁻³ solutions, substances in their standard states.
The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero (O₂(g), C(graphite), Na(s)).
Hess's law: the total enthalpy change is independent of the route taken.
Bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic; bond-enthalpy values are averages, so answers are approximate.
Lattice enthalpy is larger for smaller ions and higher charges (MgO ≫ NaCl).
A reaction is feasible when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0; entropy increases with more gas moles, melting, boiling and dissolving.

formulas.name: Heat from calorimetry
formulas.note: m = mass of solution or water (not the solute); c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

formulas.name: Molar enthalpy change
formulas.note: n = moles of limiting reactant; the minus sign makes a temperature rise give a negative ΔH.

formulas.name: Hess's law from formation
formulas.note: Multiply each ΔH_f by its coefficient.

formulas.name: Hess's law from combustion
formulas.note: Note the reversed order compared with formation data.

formulas.name: Bond enthalpies
formulas.note: Valid for gaseous species.

formulas.name: Born–Haber cycle
formulas.formula: ΔH_f = ΔH_at(metal) + ΣIE + ΔH_at(non-metal) + ΣEA + ΔH_latt
formulas.note: ΔH_latt here is lattice formation enthalpy (negative).

formulas.name: Gibbs energy
formulas.note: Convert ΔS from J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ before combining with ΔH in kJ.

formulas.name: Crossover temperature
formulas.note: Temperature at which ΔG = 0 and feasibility changes.

formulas.name: Gibbs energy and K
formulas.note: ΔG° < 0 means K > 1.

formulas.name: Entropy change of reaction
formulas.note: Unlike ΔH_f, standard entropies of elements are not zero.

formulas.name: First law and ΔH vs ΔU
formulas.formula: ΔU = q + w; ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT
formulas.note: w = −PΔV for expansion work done by the system; Δn_g = change in moles of gas.

formulas.name: Enthalpy of neutralisation
formulas.formula: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH ≈ −57 kJ mol⁻¹
formulas.note: For strong acid with strong base; weak acids or bases give a less negative value.

shortcuts.name: Neutralisation temperature rise
shortcuts.rule: Moles of water × 57 kJ gives q; ΔT = q/(total mass × 4.18).
shortcuts.example: 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl + 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH: 0.050 mol × 57 = 2.85 kJ; ΔT = 2850/(100 × 4.18) ≈ 6.8 K.

shortcuts.name: Scaling calorimetry results
shortcuts.rule: ΔT depends on concentration, not volume: doubling both volumes at the same concentration keeps ΔT; doubling concentrations doubles ΔT.
shortcuts.example: From 6.8 K above: 100 cm³ + 100 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ still gives 6.8 K; 50 cm³ + 50 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ gives 13.6 K.

shortcuts.name: Skip the zeros
shortcuts.rule: Elements in standard states have ΔH_f = 0, so leave them out of the sum.
shortcuts.example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l) with ΔH_f: CO₂ −394, H₂O −286, CH₄ −75: ΔH = −394 + 2(−286) − (−75) = −891 kJ mol⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: ΔG sign grid
shortcuts.rule: ΔH −, ΔS + always feasible; ΔH +, ΔS − never; ΔH −, ΔS − feasible at low T; ΔH +, ΔS + feasible at high T, above T = ΔH/ΔS.
shortcuts.example: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂: ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so T = 178000/161 ≈ 1106 K.

shortcuts.name: Entropy by counting gas moles
shortcuts.rule: If moles of gas increase, ΔS > 0; if they decrease, ΔS < 0.
shortcuts.example: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas, so ΔS is negative.

shortcuts.name: Manipulating equations
shortcuts.rule: Reversing an equation flips the sign of ΔH; multiplying the equation by k multiplies ΔH by k.
shortcuts.example: If H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O has ΔH = −286 kJ, then 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ has ΔH = +572 kJ.

traps: Using the mass of the solid or acid instead of the mass of the whole solution in q = mcΔT.
Forgetting the minus sign: a temperature rise means an exothermic reaction with a negative ΔH.
Combining ΔH in kJ with ΔS in J K⁻¹ without converting.
Reversing the order (products − reactants) when using combustion data.
Using bond enthalpies for liquids such as H₂O(l); the values apply to gases.
nsmqTips: Feasibility questions are usually sign questions; answer from the ΔG grid without calculating.
Know the standard definitions word for word (formation, combustion, neutralisation, atomisation, lattice); they appear as 'define' or 'name this enthalpy' riddles.
Remember −57 kJ mol⁻¹ for strong acid–strong base neutralisation; questions often ask why ethanoic acid gives a smaller value (energy is used to ionise the weak acid).

topics.summary: Kinetics studies how fast reactions go, what controls the rate and how rate depends on concentration through the rate equation. NSMQ tests order from data, half-life counting, units of k and the effects of temperature and catalysts.
keyIdeas: Collision theory: particles react only when they collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy Eₐ and with the correct orientation.
Rate increases with concentration (or pressure for gases), temperature, surface area and catalysts.
Raising temperature increases the fraction of molecules with E ≥ Eₐ (the Maxwell–Boltzmann tail), which matters far more than the extra collision frequency.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower Eₐ; it is not used up and changes neither ΔH nor the equilibrium constant.
Orders of reaction are found by experiment and are not, in general, the stoichiometric coefficients.
The rate-determining step is the slowest step in a mechanism; species in the rate equation appear in or before it.
A first-order reaction has a constant half-life, independent of starting concentration (radioactive decay is first order).

formulas.name: Rate of reaction
formulas.note: Units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

formulas.name: Rate equation
formulas.note: m and n are orders; overall order = m + n.

formulas.name: Units of k
formulas.note: Zero order mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; first s⁻¹; second dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; third dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.

formulas.name: Zero-order integrated law
formulas.note: Straight-line [A] vs t.

formulas.name: First-order integrated law
formulas.note: Straight-line ln[A] vs t.

formulas.name: Second-order integrated law
formulas.note: Straight-line 1/[A] vs t.

formulas.name: Fraction left after n half-lives
formulas.note: n = t/t½ (first order).

formulas.name: Arrhenius equation
formulas.formula: k = A e^(−Eₐ/RT); ln k = ln A − Eₐ/(RT)
formulas.note: A plot of ln k against 1/T has gradient −Eₐ/R.

formulas.name: Two-temperature Arrhenius
formulas.note: Finds Eₐ from rate constants at two temperatures.

formulas.name: Initial rate from clock reactions
formulas.note: t = time for a fixed amount of change, e.g. a cross to disappear.

shortcuts.name: Half-life counting
shortcuts.rule: Divide the time by t½ to get n, then halve n times.

shortcuts.name: Order from a concentration change
shortcuts.rule: Rate factor = (concentration factor)^order.
shortcuts.example: [A] tripled and rate × 9: 3² = 9, so second order in A. [A] doubled and rate unchanged: zero order.

shortcuts.name: 10-degree rule of thumb
shortcuts.rule: Near room temperature, rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise (for Eₐ of about 50 kJ mol⁻¹).
shortcuts.example: 20 °C → 60 °C is four 10 °C rises: rate × 2⁴ ≈ 16.

shortcuts.name: Half-life fingerprint
shortcuts.rule: How t½ responds to halving [A]₀: unchanged → first order; doubles → second order; halves → zero order.
shortcuts.example: t½ goes from 40 s to 80 s when [A]₀ is halved → second order.

shortcuts.name: Order from the units of k
shortcuts.rule: Read the order straight off the units.
shortcuts.example: k = 3.0 × 10⁻³ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ → second order; k in s⁻¹ → first order.

shortcuts.name: Powers of two for fractions
shortcuts.rule: 1/8 left = 3 half-lives; 1/16 = 4; 1/1024 ≈ 0.1% = 10 half-lives.
shortcuts.example: First-order t½ = 6 min; time for 87.5% to react (1/8 left) = 3 × 6 = 18 min.

traps: Taking the order from the balanced equation instead of from experimental data.
Saying a catalyst shifts equilibrium or changes ΔH; it only speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally.
Thinking a higher temperature only speeds up endothermic reactions; it increases the rate of every reaction.
Using t½ = 0.693/k for a reaction that is not first order.
Explaining the temperature effect only by 'more collisions'; the key reason is more collisions with energy ≥ Eₐ.
nsmqTips: For data tables, find two runs where only one concentration changes and compare factors; you rarely need to calculate k.
When a question mentions a constant half-life or radioactive decay, think first order immediately.
Be ready to sketch or describe a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve: at higher T the peak lowers and shifts right, the area stays the same, and the tail beyond Eₐ grows.

topics.summary: In a reversible reaction in a closed system, forward and reverse rates become equal and the composition stops changing; the equilibrium constant measures where that balance lies. NSMQ tests Le Chatelier predictions, K expressions, Kp–Kc relations and short ICE-table calculations.
keyIdeas: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates, and it needs a closed system.
Pure solids and pure liquids do not appear in K expressions (e.g. K for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) is Kp = p(CO₂)).
Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to partly oppose an imposed change in concentration, pressure or temperature.
Only temperature changes the value of K. For exothermic reactions K falls as T rises; for endothermic reactions K rises.
A catalyst does not change K or the equilibrium position; it only lets equilibrium be reached faster.
Large K (≫ 1) means products dominate; small K (≪ 1) means reactants dominate.
Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH < 0) uses about 450 °C, 200 atm and an iron catalyst as a compromise between yield and rate; Contact process uses V₂O₅.

formulas.name: Concentration equilibrium constant
formulas.note: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, using equilibrium concentrations.

formulas.name: Pressure equilibrium constant
formulas.note: Partial pressures of gases.

formulas.name: Kp–Kc relation
formulas.note: Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants.

formulas.name: Reaction quotient
formulas.formula: Q has the same form as K but uses current values
formulas.note: Q < K: shifts forward; Q > K: shifts backward; Q = K: at equilibrium.

formulas.name: Manipulating K
formulas.formula: reverse: K' = 1/K; multiply by n: K' = Kⁿ; add two reactions: K = K₁ × K₂
formulas.note: Follows from how the expression is built.

formulas.name: Gibbs energy and K
formulas.note: K > 1 when ΔG° < 0.

formulas.name: van 't Hoff equation
formulas.note: Temperature dependence of K.

formulas.name: Degree of dissociation (PCl₅ type)
formulas.formula: PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂: Kp = α²P / (1 − α²)
formulas.note: α = fraction dissociated, P = total pressure.

shortcuts.name: Count gas moles for pressure changes
shortcuts.rule: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles; equal moles means pressure has no effect.
shortcuts.example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: 4 → 2, so high pressure favours NH₃. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: 2 → 2, no effect.

shortcuts.name: Kp = Kc when Δn = 0
shortcuts.rule: If gas moles are equal on both sides, Kp = Kc and K has no units.
shortcuts.example: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: Δn = 0, so Kp = Kc. N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂: Δn = 1, Kp = Kc(RT).

shortcuts.name: Reverse and power
shortcuts.rule: Reverse → reciprocal; double the equation → square.
shortcuts.example: A ⇌ B has K = 4; then 2B ⇌ 2A has K = 1/4² = 1/16.

shortcuts.name: Square-root trick for symmetric ICE tables
shortcuts.rule: When the K expression is a perfect square, take √K to get a linear equation.
shortcuts.example: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K = 64, start with 1 mol each in 1 dm³: √64 = 8 = 2x/(1 − x) → x = 0.8, so [HI] = 1.6 mol dm⁻³. Check: 1.6²/0.2² = 64.

shortcuts.name: Temperature direction from ΔH
shortcuts.rule: Treat heat as a product (exothermic) or reactant (endothermic) and apply Le Chatelier.
shortcuts.example: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH = −197 kJ: heating shifts left and lowers K.

traps: Saying a catalyst increases yield; it does not change the equilibrium position.
Thinking adding an inert gas at constant volume shifts the equilibrium; partial pressures are unchanged, so nothing happens.
Including solids or pure liquids (CaCO₃(s), H₂O(l) as solvent) in K.
Saying a change of concentration or pressure changes K; only temperature does.
Confusing 'position shifts right' with 'rate increases'; they are different ideas.
nsmqTips: For Le Chatelier questions, state the direction and the reason in one breath: 'shifts right, fewer gas moles'.
Industrial conditions (Haber: Fe, ~450 °C, ~200 atm; Contact: V₂O₅, ~450 °C, 1–2 atm) are frequent recall questions.
When asked for the units of Kc, count concentration terms: (mol dm⁻³)^Δn.

topics.summary: This topic covers the definitions of acids and bases, the strength of acids and bases, the pH scale, buffers, indicators and the kinds of salts and their behaviour in water. NSMQ asks rapid pH calculations, conjugate-pair identification and predictions of salt pH.
keyIdeas: Arrhenius: acids give H⁺ in water, bases give OH⁻. Brønsted–Lowry: acids donate protons, bases accept them. Lewis: acids accept electron pairs, bases donate them.
A conjugate acid–base pair differs by one H⁺ (NH₄⁺/NH₃, H₂O/OH⁻, H₃O⁺/H₂O).
Strong acids ionise fully (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ first proton); weak acids ionise partly (CH₃COOH, H₂CO₃). Strength is not the same as concentration.
Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so neutral water has pH 7 only at 25 °C; Kw rises with temperature and neutral pH falls.
A buffer (weak acid + its salt, or weak base + its salt) resists pH change on adding small amounts of acid or base.
Indicators: methyl orange changes at pH ≈ 3.1–4.4 (strong acid–weak base titrations); phenolphthalein at ≈ 8.2–10 (weak acid–strong base).
Salt types: normal (NaCl), acid (NaHSO₄), basic (Mg(OH)Cl), double (alums such as KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O), complex (K₄[Fe(CN)₆]).

formulas.name: Ionic product of water
formulas.note: At 25 °C.

formulas.name: Acid dissociation constant
formulas.note: Smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

formulas.name: Weak acid pH
formulas.note: Valid when ionisation is small (below about 5%).

formulas.name: Weak base
formulas.note: Then pH = 14 − pOH.

formulas.name: Conjugate pair relation
formulas.note: For a conjugate acid–base pair at 25 °C.

formulas.name: Henderson–Hasselbalch
formulas.note: Buffer pH; equals pKa when [A⁻] = [HA].

formulas.name: Ostwald dilution law
formulas.note: Degree of ionisation of a weak acid rises as it is diluted.

formulas.name: Strong acid dilution
formulas.note: Holds until the pH approaches 7; water then dominates.

formulas.name: Salt of weak acid + strong base
formulas.note: Hydrolysis of A⁻ makes the solution basic (25 °C).

shortcuts.name: Power of ten gives pH
shortcuts.rule: For [H⁺] = 10⁻ⁿ, pH = n.
shortcuts.example: 0.01 mol dm⁻³ HCl: pH 2. 0.005 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ (both protons counted): [H⁺] = 0.01, pH 2.

shortcuts.name: Log 2, 3, 5
shortcuts.rule: log 2 = 0.30, log 3 = 0.48, log 5 = 0.70; pH of a × 10⁻ⁿ = n − log a.

shortcuts.name: Weak acid in one line
shortcuts.rule: pH = ½(pKa − log c).
shortcuts.example: 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid, pKa = 4.74: pH = ½(4.74 + 1) = 2.87.

shortcuts.name: Bases via pOH
shortcuts.rule: Find [OH⁻], take pOH, subtract from 14; count OH⁻ per formula unit.
shortcuts.example: 0.05 mol dm⁻³ Ba(OH)₂: [OH⁻] = 0.10, pOH 1, pH 13.

shortcuts.name: Salt pH from its parents
shortcuts.rule: The stronger parent wins: strong acid + weak base → acidic; weak acid + strong base → basic; strong + strong → neutral.
shortcuts.example: NH₄Cl acidic, CH₃COONa basic, Na₂CO₃ basic, NaCl neutral.

shortcuts.name: Half-equivalence point
shortcuts.rule: Halfway to the equivalence point in a weak acid–strong base titration, pH = pKa.
shortcuts.example: Ethanoic acid titrated with NaOH: halfway, pH = 4.74.

traps: Saying 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³ HCl has pH 8; an acid cannot be basic. Water's own H⁺ dominates and the pH is about 6.98.
Calling a concentrated weak acid 'strong'; strength means extent of ionisation.
Forgetting that diprotic acids and bases such as H₂SO₄ and Ba(OH)₂ release two H⁺ or OH⁻.
Assuming every salt is neutral.
Taking pH 7 as neutral at any temperature.
nsmqTips: Memorise log 2, 3 and 5; nearly every pH answer needs one of them.
For 'identify the conjugate base' questions, remove one H⁺ and lower the charge by one: H₂PO₄⁻ → HPO₄²⁻.
Indicator choice is a common one-word answer: strong acid–weak base → methyl orange; weak acid–strong base → phenolphthalein; weak–weak → no suitable indicator.

topics.summary: This topic covers how much of a sparingly soluble ionic solid dissolves, expressed as the solubility product Ksp, and how common ions and mixing affect precipitation. It underlies qualitative analysis, and NSMQ asks quick s ↔ Ksp conversions and 'will a precipitate form' questions.
keyIdeas: For a sparingly soluble salt in a saturated solution, solid and ions are in dynamic equilibrium: MₓAᵧ(s) ⇌ xMʸ⁺(aq) + yAˣ⁻(aq).
Ksp is constant at a given temperature; the solid is left out of the expression.
Molar solubility s is the moles of salt that dissolve per dm³ of saturated solution.
Precipitation occurs when the ionic product Q exceeds Ksp.
Common ion effect: adding an ion already in the salt lowers its solubility (AgCl is much less soluble in NaCl(aq) than in water).
Ksp values can be compared directly only for salts with the same formula type (AB vs AB, AB₂ vs AB₂).

Solubility rules: all Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻ salts are soluble; chlorides are soluble except AgCl and PbCl₂; sulfates are soluble except BaSO₄ and PbSO₄ (CaSO₄ only slightly soluble); carbonates and hydroxides are mostly insoluble except those of group 1 and NH₄⁺.

formulas.name: General Ksp
formulas.note: Equilibrium concentrations in a saturated solution.

formulas.name: 1 : 1 salt (AB)
formulas.note: AgCl, BaSO₄, CaCO₃.

formulas.name: 1 : 2 or 2 : 1 salt (AB₂, A₂B)
formulas.note: PbI₂, CaF₂, Ag₂CrO₄, Mg(OH)₂.

formulas.name: 1 : 3 or 3 : 1 salt
formulas.note: Fe(OH)₃, Al(OH)₃, Ag₃PO₄.

formulas.name: 2 : 3 salt (A₂B₃)
formulas.note: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ is 3 : 2, same result.

formulas.name: General formula type
formulas.note: For MₓAᵧ; generates all the rows above.

formulas.name: Precipitation test
formulas.formula: Q = [Mʸ⁺]ˣ[Aˣ⁻]ʸ using concentrations after mixing; precipitate if Q > Ksp
formulas.note: Remember the dilution on mixing.

formulas.name: Common ion (AB salt)
formulas.note: Valid when the added ion concentration ≫ s.

formulas.name: Mass solubility
formulas.note: Converts mol dm⁻³ to g dm⁻³.

formulas.name: Crystallisation from solubility curves
formulas.formula: mass deposited = (solubility at T₁ − solubility at T₂) × (mass of water / 100 g)
formulas.note: Solubility in g per 100 g water.

shortcuts.name: Formula-type coefficients
shortcuts.example: PbI₂ with s = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³: Ksp = 4 × (10⁻³)³ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹.

shortcuts.name: Common ion cut
shortcuts.rule: For an AB salt in c mol dm⁻³ of a common ion, s ≈ Ksp/c.
shortcuts.example: AgCl (Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) in 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaCl: s = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³, compared with 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ in pure water.

shortcuts.name: Halve on equal-volume mixing
shortcuts.rule: Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration before you compute Q.
shortcuts.example: 2 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ AgNO₃ + equal volume 2 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ NaCl: each 1 × 10⁻⁴, Q = 1 × 10⁻⁸ > 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ → AgCl precipitates.

shortcuts.name: Don't compare Ksp across formula types
shortcuts.rule: Convert to s first when formula types differ.
shortcuts.example: AgCl Ksp 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ → s ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻⁵; Ag₂CrO₄ Ksp 1.1 × 10⁻¹² → s = (1.1 × 10⁻¹²/4)^(1/3) ≈ 6.5 × 10⁻⁵. Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble despite the smaller Ksp.

shortcuts.name: SNAP mnemonic
shortcuts.rule: Salts of Sodium, Nitrate, Ammonium and Potassium are always soluble.
shortcuts.example: Will KNO₃ + NaCl give a precipitate? Every possible product contains Na⁺, K⁺ or NO₃⁻, so no.

shortcuts.name: Even squares for 1 : 1 salts
shortcuts.rule: If Ksp has an even power of ten, s is just the square root of each part.
shortcuts.example: BaSO₄ Ksp = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ → s = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³; × 233 g mol⁻¹ ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻³ g dm⁻³.

traps: Writing Ksp = s × 2s for PbI₂; the iodide concentration must be squared: (2s)².
Forgetting the dilution when two solutions are mixed before computing Q.
Concluding that a smaller Ksp always means lower solubility, even for different formula types.
Including the solid in the Ksp expression.
Doubling s for the common-ion source: in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ CaCl₂ the chloride concentration is 0.2 mol dm⁻³.
nsmqTips: Most questions ask s from Ksp or Ksp from s; say the formula type out loud (4s³, 27s⁴) and the answer follows.
Know the classic precipitates and colours: AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow, PbI₂ yellow, BaSO₄ white, Cu(OH)₂ blue, Fe(OH)₃ red-brown, Fe(OH)₂ green.
For 'why does adding HCl lower NaCl solubility' riddles, answer 'common ion effect' first, then explain.

topics.summary: Redox reactions transfer electrons; electrochemistry turns these reactions into cell voltages (galvanic cells) or uses electricity to drive them (electrolysis). NSMQ tests oxidation numbers, E°cell, electrolysis products and Faraday's-law calculations.
keyIdeas: Oxidation is loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation number; reduction is gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation number.
An oxidising agent is itself reduced; a reducing agent is itself oxidised.
Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode in every cell. In a galvanic cell the anode is negative; in electrolysis the anode is positive.
A more positive standard reduction potential means a stronger oxidising agent (F₂ is strongest); a more negative one means a stronger reducing agent (Li is strongest in water).
A cell reaction is feasible when E°cell > 0 (so ΔG° < 0).
Standard hydrogen electrode: Pt | H₂ (1 bar) | H⁺ (1 mol dm⁻³), E° = 0.00 V by definition.
In aqueous electrolysis, products depend on position in the series, concentration and electrode: concentrated NaCl(aq) gives H₂ at the cathode and Cl₂ at the anode; dilute gives O₂ at the anode.

formulas.name: Standard cell potential
formulas.note: Both values are standard reduction potentials; do not multiply them when balancing electrons.

formulas.name: Cell potential and Gibbs energy
formulas.note: n = moles of electrons transferred; F = 96 485 C mol⁻¹.

formulas.name: Charge
formulas.note: I in A, t in s, Q in C.

formulas.name: Faraday's first law
formulas.note: n = charge on the ion (electrons per ion discharged).

formulas.name: Faraday's second law
formulas.formula: for the same charge, moles deposited ∝ 1/n
formulas.note: Masses deposited are proportional to M/n.

formulas.name: Nernst equation
formulas.formula: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q
formulas.note: Second form at 25 °C.

formulas.name: E° and K
formulas.note: At 25 °C; large positive E° means very large K.

formulas.name: Oxidation number rules
formulas.formula: sum = 0 for a neutral compound or = the ion charge; F = −1; O = −2 (−1 in peroxides, +2 in OF₂); H = +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); group 1 = +1, group 2 = +2
formulas.note: Apply in that priority order.

formulas.name: Cell notation
formulas.formula: anode | anode electrolyte || cathode electrolyte | cathode
formulas.note: e.g. Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu; || is the salt bridge.

formulas.name: Daniell cell
formulas.note: Classic galvanic cell.

shortcuts.name: OIL RIG and AN OX, RED CAT
shortcuts.rule: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain; ANode = OXidation, REDuction = CAThode.
shortcuts.example: In Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, Zn loses electrons (oxidised, anode) and Cu²⁺ gains them (reduced, cathode).

shortcuts.name: Grams per faraday
shortcuts.rule: One faraday deposits M/n grams: Ag 108 g, Cu 31.75 g, Al 9 g.

shortcuts.name: Cells in series
shortcuts.rule: Same charge, so moles deposited are in the ratio 1/n: Ag⁺ : Cu²⁺ : Al³⁺ = 6 : 3 : 2.
shortcuts.example: 1.08 g Ag (0.010 mol) deposited → Cu deposited = 0.005 mol = 0.3175 g; Al = 0.0033 mol = 0.090 g.

shortcuts.name: Oxidation-number algebra
shortcuts.rule: Set the unknown as x and make the sum equal the charge.
shortcuts.example: Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻: 2x − 14 = −2 → x = +6. Mn in MnO₄⁻: x − 8 = −1 → x = +7.

shortcuts.name: Electron counts for titrations
shortcuts.rule: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ takes 5 e⁻; Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ takes 6 e⁻; Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ gives 1 e⁻.
shortcuts.example: Ratio MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 5. So 0.002 mol KMnO₄ oxidises 0.010 mol Fe²⁺.

shortcuts.name: Higher reduction potential is the cathode
shortcuts.rule: Put the more positive E° on the right (cathode) and subtract.
shortcuts.example: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V and Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V: E°cell = 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V, with Cu as the anode.

traps: Multiplying E° by the stoichiometric coefficient when balancing half-equations; E° is an intensive property.
Thinking the anode is always positive; it is negative in a galvanic cell.
Forgetting the charge on the ion (n) in Faraday's law: Cu²⁺ needs 2 F per mole.
Leaving time in minutes instead of seconds in Q = It.
Calling the oxidising agent the substance that is oxidised.
nsmqTips: Electrolysis product questions: for the cathode, metals below hydrogen (Cu, Ag) deposit, otherwise H₂; for the anode, concentrated halide gives halogen, otherwise O₂ (unless the anode is an active metal such as Cu, which dissolves).
Keep 96 500 C and simple multiples (965 s, 1930 C) in mind; quiz setters choose numbers that cancel cleanly.
When asked which species is the strongest oxidising or reducing agent from a list of E° values, pick the most positive for oxidising and the most negative for reducing.

topics.summary: The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number so that electron configuration, and with it properties, repeats periodically. NSMQ often gives a list of elements and asks for the one with the largest radius, highest ionisation energy or most acidic oxide, so trends and their exceptions must be automatic.
keyIdeas: Across a period nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same, so effective nuclear charge rises: radius falls, ionisation energy and electronegativity rise.
Down a group a new shell is added each period: radius increases, ionisation energy and electronegativity fall, and metallic character increases.
First ionisation energy dips from group 2 to 13 (Be > B, Mg > Al: p electron is higher in energy) and from group 15 to 16 (N > O, P > S: pairing repulsion).
Cations are smaller than their parent atoms and anions are larger; in an isoelectronic series, radius falls as Z increases.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element (Pauling 4.0), but chlorine has the most exothermic first electron affinity because the F atom is small and crowded.
Period 3 oxides go from basic (Na₂O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇).
Diagonal relationships (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si) arise from similar charge-to-size ratios.
Melting points across period 3 rise to a maximum at Si (giant covalent) and then drop for simple molecular P₄, S₈, Cl₂ and Ar.

formulas.name: Effective nuclear charge
formulas.note: S = shielding constant; simple estimate S ≈ number of inner electrons, so Na ≈ 11 − 10 = 1 and Cl ≈ 17 − 10 = 7.

formulas.name: Position from configuration
formulas.formula: period = highest n; s- and p-block group = valence electrons (p-block: 10 + valence electrons in 1–18 numbering)
formulas.note: e.g. [Ne]3s²3p⁵ → period 3, group 17.

formulas.name: First ionisation energy
formulas.note: Always endothermic; successive IEs always increase.

formulas.name: First electron affinity
formulas.note: Usually exothermic; second electron affinity (e.g. O⁻ → O²⁻) is endothermic.

formulas.name: Period 2 IE₁ order
formulas.formula: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne
formulas.note: Shows the two dips.

formulas.name: Isoelectronic radius order (10 e⁻)
formulas.formula: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺
formulas.note: More protons pull the same electrons closer.

formulas.name: Period 3 oxide character
formulas.formula: Na₂O, MgO basic → Al₂O₃ amphoteric → SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇ acidic
formulas.note: Ionic to covalent across the period.

formulas.name: Charge density
formulas.note: Explains polarising power, lattice energy trends and diagonal relationships.

shortcuts.name: Big jump finds the group
shortcuts.rule: In successive ionisation energies, the first very large jump comes after the last valence electron is removed.
shortcuts.example: IE₁ to IE₄ = 578, 1817, 2745, 11577 kJ mol⁻¹: the jump is after IE₃, so 3 valence electrons → group 13 (this is Al).

shortcuts.name: Subtract the noble gas (periods 4 and 5)
shortcuts.rule: Group number (1–18) = Z − Z of the previous noble gas.

shortcuts.name: Isoelectronic ordering
shortcuts.rule: Same electron count: more protons means smaller.
shortcuts.example: Rank S²⁻, Cl⁻, K⁺, Ca²⁺ (18 e⁻): Z = 16, 17, 19, 20, so S²⁻ > Cl⁻ > K⁺ > Ca²⁺.

shortcuts.name: Corner rule
shortcuts.rule: Bottom-left (Cs, Fr) is largest and most metallic with the lowest IE; top-right (F, excluding noble gases for electronegativity) is smallest and most electronegative.
shortcuts.example: Among Na, Mg, K, Ca the largest atom is K (lower and further left); the highest IE₁ is Mg.

shortcuts.name: Zig-zag dips
shortcuts.rule: IE₁ drops at groups 2→13 and 15→16 in every period.
shortcuts.example: Which is higher, P or S? P (group 15, half-filled 3p). Mg or Al? Mg.

traps: Saying fluorine has the highest electron affinity; chlorine does.
Forgetting the ionisation-energy dips and ranking O above N.
Comparing an atom's radius with an ion's without accounting for the lost or gained shell: Na⁺ is far smaller than Na.
Giving noble gases a Pauling electronegativity value in trend questions; they are usually excluded.
Calling Al₂O₃ basic; it is amphoteric and reacts with both acids and alkalis.
nsmqTips: When given four elements, first locate each by period and group in your head, then apply the corner rule; check for an IE exception only if two are neighbours.
Successive-IE tables are a favourite riddle; look for the jump, don't calculate anything.
Learn the period 3 sequences (radius, IE, melting point, oxide and chloride character) as a chain you can recite.

topics.summary: This topic explains how atoms are held together by ionic, covalent, dative and metallic bonds and intermolecular forces, and how electron-pair repulsion (VSEPR) sets molecular shape and polarity. NSMQ frequently asks for shapes, bond angles, hybridisation, σ/π counts and polarity of named species.
keyIdeas: Ionic bonds form by electron transfer (large electronegativity difference); covalent bonds share electron pairs; a dative bond is a shared pair supplied by one atom (NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, CO).
VSEPR: electron pairs around the central atom spread out to minimise repulsion. Repulsion order is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
Shape is named from atom positions only, but lone pairs still count when finding the electron-pair arrangement.
A molecule with polar bonds is nonpolar if its shape is symmetric and the outer atoms are identical (CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄, SF₆).
Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F; it explains the high boiling points of H₂O, HF and NH₃.
Intermolecular force strength: hydrogen bonds > permanent dipole–dipole > London (dispersion) forces; dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons.
Exceptions to the octet rule: BF₃ and BeCl₂ (incomplete octet); PCl₅, SF₆ and XeF₄ (expanded octet, period 3 and beyond).
Molecular orbital theory explains why O₂ is paramagnetic (two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals).

formulas.name: Steric number (electron pairs on central atom)
formulas.note: V = valence electrons of central atom; M = number of monovalent atoms bonded (H, halogens); q = ion charge with sign (+1 for NH₄⁺, −2 for SO₄²⁻). Divalent O and S atoms add 0.

formulas.name: Lone pairs
formulas.formula: lone pairs = SN − number of atoms bonded to the centre
formulas.note: Decides the shape within each arrangement.

formulas.name: Basic shapes
formulas.formula: SN 2 linear 180°; 3 trigonal planar 120°; 4 tetrahedral 109.5°; 5 trigonal bipyramidal 90° and 120°; 6 octahedral 90°
formulas.note: Arrangements when there are no lone pairs.

formulas.name: Shapes with lone pairs
formulas.formula: SN 3, 1 LP bent (<120°); SN 4, 1 LP trigonal pyramidal (~107°); SN 4, 2 LP bent (~104.5°); SN 5, 1 LP see-saw; 2 LP T-shaped; 3 LP linear; SN 6, 1 LP square pyramidal; 2 LP square planar
formulas.note: Examples: SO₂, NH₃, H₂O, SF₄, ClF₃, XeF₂, BrF₅, XeF₄.

formulas.name: Hybridisation
formulas.formula: SN 2 → sp; 3 → sp²; 4 → sp³; 5 → sp³d; 6 → sp³d²
formulas.note: Matches the steric number.

formulas.name: σ and π bonds
formulas.note: π bonds come from sideways overlap of p orbitals.

formulas.name: Formal charge
formulas.note: The best Lewis structure keeps formal charges small.

formulas.name: Bond order (MO theory)
formulas.formula: bond order = ½(bonding electrons − antibonding electrons)
formulas.note: Higher bond order: shorter and stronger bond.

formulas.name: Dipole moment
formulas.note: Units C m or debye (1 D ≈ 3.34 × 10⁻³⁰ C m).

formulas.name: Electronegativity guide
formulas.formula: Δχ > about 1.7 mainly ionic; 0.4–1.7 polar covalent; < 0.4 nonpolar covalent
formulas.note: A rough guide, not a sharp boundary.

shortcuts.name: Steric number in one line
shortcuts.rule: SN = ½(V + M − q), then subtract bonded atoms to get lone pairs.
shortcuts.example: XeF₄: ½(8 + 4) = 6, 2 LP → square planar. ClF₃: ½(7 + 3) = 5, 2 LP → T-shaped. I₃⁻: ½(7 + 2 + 1) = 5, 3 LP → linear.

shortcuts.name: Isoelectronic means same shape
shortcuts.rule: Species with the same number of atoms and valence electrons share a shape.
shortcuts.example: CO₂, N₂O, NO₂⁺ and N₃⁻ (16 valence e⁻) are all linear; CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻ and BF₃ (24 valence e⁻) are all trigonal planar.

shortcuts.name: σ/π counting
shortcuts.rule: Every bond gives one σ; add one π for each extra bond in a double or triple bond.
shortcuts.example: Ethyne H–C≡C–H: 3σ, 2π. Benzene C₆H₆: 6 C–C σ + 6 C–H σ = 12σ, 3π.

shortcuts.name: Lone pairs squeeze the angle
shortcuts.rule: From 109.5°, each lone pair cuts roughly 2.5°.

shortcuts.name: Bond order from electron count (second-period diatomics)
shortcuts.rule: 14 total electrons → bond order 3; each electron above 14 (up to 20) lowers it by ½; each electron below 14 (down to 10) also lowers it by ½.

shortcuts.name: Symmetry test for polarity
shortcuts.rule: Identical outer atoms in a symmetric shape with no lone pairs on the centre (or symmetric lone pairs, as in XeF₄) → nonpolar.
shortcuts.example: CCl₄, BF₃, SF₆, XeF₄ nonpolar; CHCl₃, NH₃, SO₂ polar.

traps: Naming the shape from the electron-pair arrangement: NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal, not tetrahedral.
Calling a molecule polar just because its bonds are polar (CO₂ and CCl₄ are nonpolar).
Claiming hydrogen bonding in CH₄ or HCl; H must be bonded to N, O or F.
Forcing an octet on boron in BF₃; boron has only six valence electrons there.
Forgetting that a double or triple bond counts as one electron-pair region in VSEPR.
nsmqTips: For 'shape of X' questions, say steric number → lone pairs → shape in your head; the one-line SN formula handles ions like NH₄⁺, ClO₄⁻ and ICl₄⁻ in seconds.
Have bond angles ready as numbers (180, 120, 109.5, 107, 104.5, 90); quiz setters often ask for the angle rather than the shape name.
In boiling-point comparison questions, check for hydrogen bonding first, then molar mass for dispersion forces.

topics.summary: The preparation, properties, tests and industrial manufacture of the important non-metals and their compounds: hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulphur, the halogens and the noble gases. NSMQ loves this topic for quick-fire questions on industrial conditions, catalysts, gas tests and oxidation states.
keyIdeas: Non-metals are mostly electronegative; they form acidic or neutral oxides (CO₂, SO₂, SO₃, NO₂, P₄O₁₀ are acidic; CO, NO, N₂O are neutral).
Halogen reactivity and oxidising power fall down Group 17 (F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂); a halogen displaces any halide below it from solution.
Allotropes: carbon (diamond, graphite, fullerenes, graphene), sulphur (rhombic stable below about 96 °C, monoclinic above), phosphorus (white, red), oxygen (O₂, O₃).
Graphite conducts because each C uses three electrons in σ-bonds and the fourth is delocalised between layers; diamond (four bonds per C) does not.
Concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as an acid, a dehydrating agent, a drying agent and an oxidising agent.
Chlorine bleaches only when moist: HOCl oxidises the dye (permanent). SO₂ bleaches by reduction (temporary).
Nitrogen spans oxidation states −3 (NH₃) to +5 (HNO₃, N₂O₅).
Noble gases are unreactive because their valence shells are full; Xe still forms fluorides and oxides such as XeF₂, XeF₄ and XeO₃.

formulas.name: Haber process
formulas.note: Iron catalyst, about 450 °C, about 200 atm. The forward reaction is exothermic, and 4 volumes of gas give 2.

formulas.name: Contact process
formulas.note: V₂O₅ catalyst, about 450 °C, 1–2 atm. SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ to give oleum (H₂S₂O₇), which is then diluted with water.

formulas.name: Ostwald process
formulas.note: Pt–Rh gauze catalyst, about 850 °C, for the first step.

formulas.name: Laboratory ammonia
formulas.note: Heat the mixture. Dry over CaO (quicklime) and collect by upward delivery.

formulas.name: Laboratory chlorine
formulas.note: Concentrated HCl, warmed. Pass the gas through water (removes HCl), then conc H₂SO₄ (dries it), and collect by downward delivery.

formulas.name: Laboratory oxygen
formulas.note: MnO₂ is only a catalyst and is unchanged at the end.

formulas.name: Chlorine and water
formulas.note: HOCl (chloric(I) acid) is the bleaching and disinfecting species.

formulas.name: Chlorine and NaOH
formulas.formula: Cold, dilute: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O; hot, concentrated: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O
formulas.note: Disproportionation: Cl goes from 0 to −1 and +1 (cold), or to −1 and +5 (hot).

formulas.name: Dehydration by conc H₂SO₄
formulas.note: Sugar chars to black carbon. The acid removes H and O in a 2:1 ratio.

formulas.name: Water gas
formulas.formula: C + H₂O → CO + H₂ (over white-hot coke)
formulas.note: Industrial source of hydrogen. The CO is then shifted: CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂.

shortcuts.name: Halogen ladder for displacement
shortcuts.rule: Write F, Cl, Br, I top to bottom. A free halogen displaces only the halides below it.
shortcuts.example: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ (solution turns orange-brown). I₂ + KCl gives no reaction because I is below Cl.

shortcuts.name: Compare with air (Mr 29) to pick a collection method
shortcuts.rule: Mr < 29 means the gas is lighter than air: collect by upward delivery. Mr > 29 means downward delivery. Collect over water only if the gas is insoluble.
shortcuts.example: NH₃ (17): upward, and never over water because it is very soluble. Cl₂ (71) and HCl (36.5): downward. H₂ and O₂: over water.

shortcuts.name: Nitrogen oxidation-state ladder
shortcuts.rule: Memorise NH₃ −3, N₂H₄ −2, NH₂OH −1, N₂ 0, N₂O +1, NO +2, N₂O₃/HNO₂ +3, NO₂ +4, N₂O₅/HNO₃ +5.
shortcuts.example: HNO₂: H is +1 and 2 O are −4, so N = +3. It sits in the middle, so HNO₂ can act as an oxidising or a reducing agent.

shortcuts.name: Gas-test mnemonic
shortcuts.rule: Pop–Relight–Milky–Blue–Bleach–Green: H₂ squeaky pop, O₂ relights a glowing splint, CO₂ turns limewater milky, NH₃ turns damp red litmus blue, Cl₂ bleaches damp litmus, SO₂ turns acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ from orange to green.
shortcuts.example: A gas turns orange dichromate paper green and smells choking: SO₂. A gas bleaches damp blue litmus after first turning it red: Cl₂.

shortcuts.name: Process–catalyst pairs
shortcuts.rule: Fe for Haber, V₂O₅ for Contact, Pt–Rh for Ostwald, Ni for hydrogenation. All three big processes run near 450 °C, except Ostwald (about 850 °C).
shortcuts.example: Asked for the catalyst in making H₂SO₄, answer V₂O₅ (vanadium(V) oxide) at once. Pt is the older, easily poisoned alternative.

shortcuts.name: Le Chatelier on gas volumes
shortcuts.rule: Count gas moles on each side. Fewer moles on the product side means high pressure raises the yield. An exothermic forward reaction means low temperature raises the yield, and the industrial temperature is a compromise with rate.
shortcuts.example: Haber: 4 → 2 moles, so high pressure helps. ΔH is negative, so low temperature favours yield, but 450 °C is used for speed.

traps: Drying NH₃ with conc H₂SO₄ or anhydrous CaCl₂: both react with it. Use CaO.
Saying SO₃ is dissolved directly in water in the Contact process. That forms a corrosive acid mist, so it is absorbed in conc H₂SO₄ instead.
Assuming metals with HNO₃ give H₂. Concentrated HNO₃ usually gives NO₂ and dilute HNO₃ gives NO, because nitrate is the oxidant. Only Mg and Mn with very dilute acid give H₂.
Thinking HF is a strong acid because F is the most electronegative halogen. HF is a weak acid (strong H–F bond and H-bonding).
Confusing the bleaching mechanisms: Cl₂/HOCl bleaches by oxidation (permanent), SO₂ by reduction (colour can return).
nsmqTips: Industrial-process questions almost always ask for catalyst, temperature, pressure, or why a compromise is used. Learn them as a three-line table.
For 'identify the gas' riddles, listen for the test result word (pop, relights, milky, blue, bleaches, green) and answer from the mnemonic.
When asked for an oxidation state, use the H = +1, O = −2 bookkeeping out loud only if you are stuck. Otherwise recall the nitrogen and sulphur ladders (S: −2 in H₂S, +4 in SO₂, +6 in H₂SO₄).

topics.summary: How metals are obtained from their ores, how the extraction method follows from the reactivity series, and how metals corrode and are protected. Ghana's gold, bauxite, manganese and diamonds make this a favourite NSMQ topic, alongside the blast furnace and electrolysis calculations.
keyIdeas: Extraction method depends on reactivity: K to Al are extracted by electrolysis of molten compounds; Zn, Fe, Sn and Pb by reduction with C or CO; Cu and Hg by roasting or heating; Ag and Au often occur native.
Ore processing steps: concentration (froth flotation, magnetic separation, washing), conversion (roasting sulphides or calcining carbonates to oxides), reduction, then refining.
In the blast furnace, CO is the main reducing agent. Limestone removes silica as slag (CaSiO₃), and pig iron contains about 4% carbon.

Aluminium: bauxite is purified to Al₂O₃ (Bayer process), dissolved in molten cryolite and electrolysed with carbon electrodes (Hall–Héroult). Ghana's smelter is VALCO at Tema, and bauxite is mined at Awaso.
Copper is purified electrolytically: impure Cu anode, pure Cu cathode, CuSO₄ electrolyte. Ag and Au collect as anode sludge.
Rusting needs both water and oxygen and is speeded up by salt. Prevention: barrier methods (paint, oil, plating) or sacrificial protection with Zn or Mg (galvanising, sacrificial anodes).
Ghana resources: gold (Obuasi, Tarkwa), manganese (Nsuta), bauxite (Awaso, Nyinahin), diamonds (Akwatia).

formulas.name: Blast furnace reactions
formulas.formula: C + O₂ → CO₂; CO₂ + C → 2CO; Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
formulas.note: Coke burns to give heat and then CO, which reduces the haematite.

formulas.name: Slag formation
formulas.formula: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃
formulas.note: Basic CaO removes acidic silica impurity as molten slag, which floats on the iron.

formulas.name: Hall–Héroult electrolysis
formulas.note: Al₂O₃ in molten Na₃AlF₆ (cryolite) at about 950 °C. The carbon anodes burn away (C + O₂ → CO₂) and must be replaced.

formulas.name: Bayer process
formulas.note: Amphoteric Al₂O₃ dissolves; Fe₂O₃ does not and is filtered off as red mud. Al(OH)₃ is then precipitated and heated to give pure Al₂O₃.

formulas.name: Downs process (sodium)
formulas.formula: Cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; Anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
formulas.note: Molten NaCl with CaCl₂ added to lower the melting point to about 600 °C.

formulas.name: Roasting sulphide ores
formulas.note: Converts sulphide to oxide before reduction: ZnO + C → Zn + CO.

formulas.name: Gold cyanidation
formulas.note: Gold dissolves as a cyanide complex and is recovered by zinc displacement or activated carbon.

formulas.name: Faraday's law
formulas.note: m in g, I in A, t in s, n = electrons per ion. One faraday deposits M/n grams.

formulas.name: Rusting
formulas.note: Hydrated iron(III) oxide. Electrochemical: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ at anodic sites, O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ at cathodic sites.

formulas.name: Common ores
formulas.formula: Bauxite Al₂O₃·2H₂O; haematite Fe₂O₃; magnetite Fe₃O₄; siderite FeCO₃; malachite CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂; chalcopyrite CuFeS₂; galena PbS; zinc blende ZnS; cassiterite SnO₂; cinnabar HgS; pyrolusite MnO₂
formulas.note: Name-to-formula questions are common. Learn them in pairs.

shortcuts.name: Reactivity series mnemonic
shortcuts.rule: Please Stop Calling Me A Careless Zebra, Instead Try Learning How Copper Saves Gold = K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, Sn (tin), Pb (lead), H, Cu, Ag, Au.
shortcuts.example: Is Mg extracted by carbon? Mg sits above C (the 'Careless') so no, it needs electrolysis. Sn is below C, so carbon reduction works.

shortcuts.name: Mass per faraday = M/n
shortcuts.rule: Divide molar mass by ion charge once, then scale by the number of faradays.

shortcuts.name: Same charge, compare moles of metal
shortcuts.rule: Metals deposited by the same charge are in moles proportional to 1/n.
shortcuts.example: The same current runs through Ag⁺, Cu²⁺ and Al³⁺ cells in series: moles are in the ratio 6 : 3 : 2 (1/1 : 1/2 : 1/3 scaled by 6).

shortcuts.name: Percent metal in an ore
shortcuts.rule: Memorise the big three: Fe₂O₃ is 70% Fe (112/160), Fe₃O₄ is about 72.4% Fe (168/232), Al₂O₃ is about 52.9% Al (54/102).
shortcuts.example: Maximum Fe from 1 tonne of pure haematite = 0.70 tonne = 700 kg.

shortcuts.name: Sacrificial protection test
shortcuts.rule: The coating protects iron after scratching only if it is MORE reactive than Fe (higher in the series).
shortcuts.example: Galvanised (Zn) bucket scratched: Zn corrodes, iron is safe. Tin-plated can scratched: iron corrodes faster than if bare, because Fe is more reactive than Sn.

traps: Calling cryolite a catalyst. It is a solvent that lowers the operating temperature from about 2050 °C (m.p. of Al₂O₃) and improves conductivity.
Saying coke directly reduces Fe₂O₃ as the main step. CO is the main reductant; limestone is for slag, not reduction.
Thinking aluminium is unreactive because it does not corrode. Its thin, tough Al₂O₃ layer protects it, but Al is high in the series.
Forgetting that Downs and Hall–Héroult use MOLTEN electrolytes. Electrolysing aqueous NaCl gives H₂ at the cathode, not Na.
Mixing up anode and cathode in copper refining: the impure copper is the anode and dissolves; pure copper plates on the cathode.
nsmqTips: When a riddle mentions Obuasi, Tarkwa, Nsuta, Awaso or Akwatia, the answer is gold, gold, manganese, bauxite/aluminium and diamond.
For electrolysis calculations, convert charge to faradays first (divide by 96 500). Numbers like 965, 9650 and 19 300 C are deliberately chosen to give 0.01, 0.1 and 0.2 F.
'Why is X extracted by electrolysis?' has a one-line answer: X is above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce its oxide.

topics.summary: The d-block elements, their electronic configurations, variable oxidation states, colour, magnetism and catalytic activity, and the coordination compounds they form, explained with crystal field theory. NSMQ uses it for configuration quick-fires and magnetic-moment calculations; university courses extend it to CFSE, isomerism and the 18-electron rule.
keyIdeas: A transition element has, or forms an ion with, an incomplete d subshell. Zn is excluded (Zn and Zn²⁺ are both d¹⁰). Many school syllabuses also exclude Sc because Sc³⁺ is d⁰, although the Sc atom (3d¹) meets the IUPAC definition.
Exceptions to the filling order: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹, because half-filled and filled d subshells are extra stable.
On ionisation, 4s electrons are lost before 3d: Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵.

In an octahedral field the d orbitals split into a lower t₂g set (3) and an upper e_g set (2), separated by Δo. Colour arises from d–d transitions absorbing visible light; the observed colour is the complement.
Spectrochemical series (weak to strong field): I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < NO₂⁻ < CN⁻ < CO. Strong-field ligands favour low-spin complexes.
Coordination number = number of donor atoms bonded to the metal: 2 linear, 4 tetrahedral or square planar (d⁸ Ni²⁺, Pd²⁺, Pt²⁺ with strong ligands), 6 octahedral.
Chelating ligands (en, C₂O₄²⁻, EDTA⁴⁻) bind through several donor atoms and form extra-stable complexes (chelate effect, entropy-driven).

Transition metals and their compounds are catalysts because they have variable oxidation states and surfaces that adsorb reactants: Fe (Haber), V₂O₅ (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation), MnO₂ (H₂O₂ decomposition).

formulas.name: Spin-only magnetic moment
formulas.note: n = number of unpaired electrons; BM = Bohr magnetons. Good for first-row ions.

formulas.name: Octahedral CFSE
formulas.formula: CFSE = (−0.4x + 0.6y)Δo (+ pairing energy for each extra pair forced)
formulas.note: x = electrons in t₂g, y = electrons in e_g.

formulas.name: Tetrahedral splitting
formulas.note: e set lower, t₂ set upper (inverted). Δt is small, so tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin.

formulas.name: Metal oxidation state
formulas.formula: Oxidation state of M = overall charge − Σ(ligand charges)
formulas.note: Neutral ligands: H₂O, NH₃, CO, en. Anionic: Cl⁻, CN⁻, OH⁻, C₂O₄²⁻ (2−), EDTA (4−).

formulas.name: d-electron count
formulas.formula: dⁿ: n = group number − oxidation state (groups 3–12)
formulas.note: For the 3d series. Fe³⁺: 8 − 3 = d⁵.

formulas.name: Effective atomic number (EAN)
formulas.formula: EAN = Z − oxidation state + 2 × (number of donor atoms)
formulas.note: Stable complexes often reach the next noble-gas number (36 for 3d metals).

formulas.name: 18-electron rule
formulas.formula: Metal valence electrons (group number for M⁰) + 2 per σ-donor ligand (± charge) = 18
formulas.note: Works best for organometallics and carbonyls such as Ni(CO)₄, Fe(CO)₅, Cr(CO)₆.

formulas.name: Splitting energy from absorption
formulas.formula: Δo = hc/λ per ion; per mole E (kJ mol⁻¹) ≈ 119 600 / λ(nm)
formulas.note: λ = wavelength of maximum absorption.

formulas.name: Naming complexes
formulas.formula: Ligands (alphabetical, with di/tri/tetra) then metal (oxidation state in Roman numerals); anionic complexes end in -ate
formulas.note: e.g. [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ tetraamminecopper(II); [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ hexacyanoferrate(III); [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ diamminesilver(I).

shortcuts.name: Memorise the μ table
shortcuts.example: [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺, high-spin d⁵ with 5 unpaired: 5.92 BM. [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, low-spin t₂g⁵ with 1 unpaired: 1.73 BM.

shortcuts.name: Group minus oxidation state
shortcuts.rule: Get the d count without writing configurations: dⁿ = group − oxidation state.
shortcuts.example: MnO₄⁻: Mn is +7, group 7, so d⁰, and its purple colour is charge transfer, not d–d. [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺: 9 − 3 = d⁶, low spin, so diamagnetic (μ = 0).

shortcuts.name: d⁰ / d¹⁰ means colourless
shortcuts.rule: No partly filled d subshell means no d–d transition, so the compound is white or colourless (unless charge transfer occurs).
shortcuts.example: Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰), Sc³⁺ (d⁰), Ti⁴⁺ (d⁰), Cu⁺ (d¹⁰), Ag⁺ (d¹⁰): ZnSO₄ and CuCl are white.

shortcuts.name: CFSE quick values
shortcuts.rule: Octahedral, ignoring pairing energy: d³ −1.2Δo; d⁵ high spin 0; d⁶ low spin −2.4Δo; d⁸ −1.2Δo; d¹⁰ 0.
shortcuts.example: Why is Cr³⁺ (d³) so inert in octahedral complexes? It has a large CFSE (−1.2Δo) with three unpaired electrons, one in each t₂g orbital.

shortcuts.name: Isomer counting by formula type
shortcuts.rule: Octahedral MA₄B₂: 2 (cis/trans). MA₃B₃: 2 (fac/mer). [M(AA)₃]: one pair of optical isomers. cis-[M(AA)₂B₂] is chiral, trans is not. Square planar MA₂B₂: 2 (cis/trans), never optical.
shortcuts.example: [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] has 2 isomers; the cis form is the anticancer drug cisplatin.

shortcuts.name: 18-electron check
shortcuts.rule: For a neutral metal carbonyl, metal group number + 2 × (number of CO) should equal 18.
shortcuts.example: Ni(CO)₄: 10 + 8 = 18. Fe(CO)₅: 8 + 10 = 18. Cr(CO)₆: 6 + 12 = 18. So the formula of the stable chromium carbonyl must be Cr(CO)₆.

traps: Writing Fe²⁺ as [Ar]3d⁴4s². The 4s electrons go first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶.
Counting ligands instead of donor atoms for coordination number: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ has 3 ligands but coordination number 6.
Explaining KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇ colour by d–d transitions. Both are d⁰; the colour comes from ligand-to-metal charge transfer.
Assuming every strong-field complex is low spin. Low spin happens only when Δo exceeds the pairing energy, and only for d⁴–d⁷ octahedral is there a choice.
Confusing the colour absorbed with the colour seen: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs orange-red light and looks blue.
nsmqTips: 'Write the electronic configuration of Cr / Cu / Fe³⁺' is a classic 10-second question. Have the exceptions and the ion rule ready.
For magnetic-moment questions, count unpaired electrons first (using high or low spin), then quote the table value. Do not try to compute square roots live.
For naming, say the ligands alphabetically, ignoring multiplying prefixes (ammine before chlorido), then the metal with -ate for anions: ferrate, cuprate, argentate, aurate, plumbate, stannate.

topics.summary: The IUPAC rules for naming organic compounds, and the types of isomerism: structural (chain, position, functional group) and stereoisomerism (geometric and optical). NSMQ often gives a structure to name, or asks how many isomers a formula has, so counting tricks pay off.
keyIdeas: Name = prefix (substituents with locants) + root (longest chain containing the main functional group) + suffix (main functional group).
Number the chain so the principal functional group, then multiple bonds, then substituents get the lowest locants. Substituents are listed alphabetically.
Priority of suffix groups: carboxylic acid > ester > acyl chloride > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine. Halo, nitro and alkyl groups are always prefixes.
Structural isomers share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity: chain, position or functional group isomers (alcohol/ether, aldehyde/ketone, acid/ester, alkene/cycloalkane).
Geometric (cis/trans or E/Z) isomerism needs restricted rotation (C=C or a ring) AND two different groups on each of the two carbons.

Optical isomerism needs a chiral molecule, usually a carbon with four different groups. Enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions; a 50:50 racemic mixture is optically inactive.
E/Z uses Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priorities (higher atomic number first). Z means the two higher-priority groups are on the same side.

formulas.name: Chain-length roots
formulas.formula: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6, hept 7, oct 8, non 9, dec 10
formulas.note: The root counts the carbons in the main chain.

formulas.name: General formulas
formulas.formula: Alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; alkene and cycloalkane CₙH₂ₙ; alkyne CₙH₂ₙ₋₂; alkanol CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH; aldehyde/ketone CₙH₂ₙO; acid/ester CₙH₂ₙO₂
formulas.note: Isomers share a general formula across classes (e.g. acids and esters).

formulas.name: Degree of unsaturation (DBE)
formulas.note: C, N, H, X = number of carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen and halogen atoms. Ignore O. Each ring or π bond counts 1.

formulas.name: Maximum stereoisomers
formulas.note: n = number of stereocentres (chiral C atoms plus stereogenic C=C). Fewer if a meso form exists.

formulas.name: Alkane structural isomer counts
formulas.formula: C₄ 2, C₅ 3, C₆ 5, C₇ 9, C₈ 18, C₉ 35, C₁₀ 75
formulas.note: Counts structural (constitutional) isomers only.

formulas.name: Alkyl group isomer counts
formulas.note: The basis for counting alcohols, haloalkanes, aldehydes and acids.

formulas.name: Ester naming
formulas.formula: R′OOC–R or RCOOR′ is named 'R′-yl R-oate'
formulas.note: The alcohol-derived part comes first: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is ethyl ethanoate; HCOOCH₃ is methyl methanoate.

formulas.name: Chiral centre condition
formulas.formula: C bonded to four different groups (Cabcd)
formulas.note: Look for a CH with three different other groups, e.g. CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.

shortcuts.name: DBE in your head
shortcuts.rule: Compare with the saturated alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: every 2 H missing = 1 ring or π bond.
shortcuts.example: C₆H₆: saturated would be C₆H₁₄, 8 H missing, so DBE = 4 (one ring + three C=C), which fits benzene. C₄H₈: DBE = 1, so it is butene or cyclobutane.

shortcuts.name: Count by alkyl group
shortcuts.rule: For R–Y with one functional group, isomers = number of alkyl isomers of R.
shortcuts.example: C₄H₉OH: C₄H₉ has 4 forms, so 4 alcohols. Add the 3 ethers (methyl propyl, methyl isopropyl, diethyl) for 7 structural isomers of C₄H₁₀O. C₅H₁₀O₂ acids = C₄H₉COOH = 4.

shortcuts.name: Ester isomer split
shortcuts.rule: Split CₙH₂ₙO₂ esters into (acid carbons, alcohol carbons) pairs and multiply alkyl counts.
shortcuts.example: C₄H₈O₂ esters: HCOOC₃H₇ (2, propyl and isopropyl) + CH₃COOC₂H₅ (1) + C₂H₅COOCH₃ (1) = 4 esters.

shortcuts.name: Geometric isomer check
shortcuts.rule: Look at each alkene carbon. If either carbon carries two identical groups, there is no cis/trans.
shortcuts.example: But-1-ene (CH₂=) has none. But-2-ene has cis and trans. 2-methylbut-2-ene has none, because one carbon carries two CH₃.

shortcuts.name: Chiral by symmetry
shortcuts.rule: Put your finger on the candidate carbon and read the four groups. If two chains going out are identical, it is not chiral.
shortcuts.example: 2-chlorobutane: H, Cl, CH₃, C₂H₅, so chiral. 3-chloropentane: H, Cl, C₂H₅, C₂H₅, so not chiral. Butan-2-ol is chiral; propan-2-ol is not.

shortcuts.name: Spot the hidden longer chain
shortcuts.rule: If a name has an ethyl on C2 or a propyl on C3, the main chain was chosen wrongly. Redraw and recount.
shortcuts.example: '2-ethylbutane' is really 3-methylpentane (6-carbon chain). '2-ethylpentane' is really 3-methylhexane.

traps: Giving a locant to the carbon of –COOH or –CHO: it is always C1, so the name is butanoic acid, not butan-1-oic acid.
Numbering from the wrong end: 3-methylbutane is wrong. The lowest-locant rule gives 2-methylbutane.
Forgetting that cycloalkanes are isomers of alkenes (C₃H₆ is propene or cyclopropane), and ethers of alcohols.
Saying a racemic mixture contains no chiral molecules. It contains equal amounts of both enantiomers, whose rotations cancel.
Using cis/trans for alkenes with three or four different substituents. Use E/Z with CIP priorities instead.
nsmqTips: 'How many isomers of C₄H₉Cl?' type questions: answer 4 at once from the alkyl table. For C₅H₁₁X the answer is 8 structural isomers.
When naming from a spoken structure, write the chain quickly as carbon numbers on paper, find the longest chain, then fix the lowest locants. Say substituents alphabetically (ethyl before methyl).
Optical-isomer questions usually hinge on one carbon. Name the four groups aloud to justify your answer.

topics.summary: Alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and benzene: their sources, preparation, reactions and tests. NSMQ asks about combustion stoichiometry, gas-volume (eudiometry) problems, tests for unsaturation and the different reactions of benzene versus alkenes.
keyIdeas: Alkanes are saturated and fairly unreactive. They undergo combustion and free-radical substitution with halogens in UV light.
Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated and undergo electrophilic addition (H₂, X₂, HX, H₂O). Alkenes decolourise bromine water and acidified or alkaline KMnO₄.
Markovnikov's rule: when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, H goes to the carbon that already has more H atoms (via the more stable carbocation).
Benzene's delocalised π system makes it resist addition. It prefers electrophilic substitution (nitration, halogenation with FeBr₃/AlCl₃, Friedel–Crafts).
Boiling points rise with chain length; branching lowers boiling point (smaller surface contact, weaker London forces).
Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation (refinery gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, bitumen). Cracking breaks long chains into shorter alkanes plus alkenes.
Terminal alkynes (with ≡C–H) give precipitates with ammoniacal AgNO₃ (white) or ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂ (red); alkenes do not.

formulas.name: General combustion
formulas.note: Complete combustion. Limited oxygen gives CO or soot.

formulas.name: Free-radical substitution
formulas.note: Initiation Cl₂ → 2Cl•; propagation Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. Gives a mixture up to CCl₄.

formulas.name: Hydrogenation
formulas.note: Ni catalyst, about 150 °C. Basis of margarine manufacture.

formulas.name: Bromine test
formulas.note: Red-brown bromine is decolourised: the test for C=C. The product is 1,2-dibromoethane.

formulas.name: Hydration of ethene
formulas.note: H₃PO₄ catalyst on silica, about 300 °C, 60–70 atm.

formulas.name: Baeyer's test
formulas.note: Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄: purple to brown (MnO₂). Product is ethane-1,2-diol.

formulas.name: Ethyne from calcium carbide
formulas.note: Laboratory and welding source of ethyne.

formulas.name: Laboratory methane
formulas.note: Heat sodium ethanoate with soda lime (decarboxylation).

formulas.name: Nitration of benzene
formulas.note: Conc HNO₃ + conc H₂SO₄, kept below about 55 °C to avoid further nitration.

formulas.name: Cracking
formulas.note: Thermal or catalytic (zeolite, Al₂O₃/SiO₂). Always produces at least one alkene.

formulas.name: Molar masses of series
formulas.formula: Alkane Mr = 14n + 2; alkene Mr = 14n; alkyne Mr = 14n − 2
formulas.note: n = number of carbon atoms.

shortcuts.name: Oxygen moles = x + y/4
shortcuts.rule: For each hydrocarbon molecule, O₂ needed = carbons + hydrogens/4. Double everything if you get a half.
shortcuts.example: C₃H₈: 3 + 2 = 5 O₂. C₈H₁₈: 8 + 4.5 = 12.5, so 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O.

shortcuts.name: Eudiometry from volumes
shortcuts.rule: Volume of CO₂ ÷ volume of hydrocarbon = x. O₂ used ÷ hydrocarbon volume = x + y/4. Solve for y.
shortcuts.example: 10 cm³ of hydrocarbon uses 50 cm³ O₂ and gives 30 cm³ CO₂: x = 3, 3 + y/4 = 5, so y = 8: C₃H₈ (propane).

shortcuts.name: Mr to formula via 14n
shortcuts.rule: Divide Mr by 14: remainder +2 means alkane, 0 means alkene, −2 (i.e. 12) means alkyne.
shortcuts.example: Mr 72: 72 = 14×5 + 2, so pentane C₅H₁₂. Mr 56 = 14×4, so butene. Mr 40 = 14×3 − 2, so propyne.

shortcuts.name: H₂ uptake counts π bonds
shortcuts.rule: Moles of H₂ (or Br₂) absorbed per mole of hydrocarbon = number of C=C equivalents (a C≡C counts 2).
shortcuts.example: 0.10 mol of a hydrocarbon takes up 4.48 dm³ H₂ at STP = 0.20 mol, so 2 π bonds: an alkyne or a diene.

shortcuts.name: Markovnikov: the rich get richer
shortcuts.rule: The carbon with more H gets the H; the X goes to the more substituted carbon.
shortcuts.example: Propene + HBr gives 2-bromopropane as the major product, not 1-bromopropane.

shortcuts.name: Sooty flame by C:H ratio
shortcuts.rule: The higher the C:H ratio, the smokier the flame.
shortcuts.example: Ethyne (C₂H₂) and benzene (C₆H₆) are both 1:1 and burn very sooty. Methane (1:4) burns with a clean blue flame.

traps: Saying benzene decolourises bromine water like an alkene. It does not; it reacts with Br₂ only with a FeBr₃ catalyst, by substitution.
Writing only CH₃Cl for methane chlorination. Free-radical substitution gives a mixture of CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄.
Applying Markovnikov to symmetrical alkenes (but-2-ene gives a single product), or forgetting the peroxide (anti-Markovnikov) effect, which works only for HBr.
In eudiometry, forgetting that liquid water takes up no volume at room temperature, and that KOH absorbs CO₂.
Thinking branched isomers boil higher: 2,2-dimethylpropane (about 10 °C) boils far lower than pentane (about 36 °C).
nsmqTips: Gas-volume combustion problems are typical riddle maths. Set x from CO₂ first; it takes 5 seconds.
'Distinguish ethene from ethane' answers: bromine water decolourised, or KMnO₄ purple to colourless/brown. 'Ethene from ethyne': ammoniacal AgNO₃ or Cu₂Cl₂ precipitate with ethyne only.
Learn catalysts and conditions as pairs: Ni for hydrogenation, H₃PO₄ for hydration, UV for substitution, FeBr₃/AlCl₃ for aromatic halogenation, conc H₂SO₄ for nitration.

topics.summary: The preparation and reactions of alkanols, alkanals and alkanones, alkanoic acids, esters, amines and haloalkanes, and the chemical tests that tell them apart. NSMQ often asks for the reagent and observation for a test, oxidation products, or ester naming.
keyIdeas: Alcohols are classed by how many carbons are attached to the C–OH carbon: primary (1), secondary (2), tertiary (3).
Oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange to green) or KMnO₄: primary alcohol gives an aldehyde, then a carboxylic acid; secondary gives a ketone; tertiary resists oxidation.
Aldehydes are reducing agents (positive Tollens' and Fehling's); ketones are not. Both give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH (Brady's reagent).
Acidity order: carboxylic acid > phenol > water > alcohol. Only acids are strong enough to release CO₂ from NaHCO₃.
Esters form from acids and alcohols (reversible, conc H₂SO₄ catalyst). They smell fruity and are hydrolysed by acid (reversible) or alkali (saponification, goes to completion).
Haloalkanes with aqueous OH⁻ undergo substitution to alcohols; with ethanolic KOH (hot) they undergo elimination to alkenes.
Amines are weak bases (lone pair on N) and form salts with acids; aliphatic amines are stronger bases than NH₃.

formulas.name: Fermentation
formulas.note: Yeast (zymase), anaerobic, about 25–37 °C. Stops at about 15% ethanol. Basis of akpeteshie and palm-wine production.

formulas.name: Esterification
formulas.note: Conc H₂SO₄ catalyst; warm. The product is ethyl ethanoate.

formulas.name: Alcohol with sodium
