formulas.note: Effervescence with any –OH compound. The product is sodium ethoxide.

formulas.name: Dehydration of ethanol
formulas.note: Excess conc H₂SO₄ at about 170 °C, or hot Al₂O₃.

formulas.name: Acid with carbonate
formulas.note: Effervescence with Na₂CO₃ or NaHCO₃ is the test for –COOH.

formulas.name: Saponification
formulas.note: Alkaline ester hydrolysis is irreversible. With fats it gives soap.

formulas.name: Haloalkane reactions
formulas.formula: R–X + OH⁻(aq) → R–OH + X⁻; CH₃CH₂Br + KOH(ethanolic) → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O
formulas.note: Aqueous gives substitution; alcoholic and hot gives elimination.

formulas.name: Amine as a base
formulas.note: Gives methylammonium chloride.

formulas.name: Tollens' and Fehling's tests
formulas.formula: Tollens' ([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺): silver mirror; Fehling's/Benedict's (Cu²⁺): blue to brick-red Cu₂O
formulas.note: Positive for aldehydes. Ketones are negative. Methanoic acid also gives a positive Tollens'.

formulas.name: Iodoform test
formulas.formula: I₂ + NaOH (warm): yellow precipitate of CHI₃ (m.p. about 119 °C)
formulas.note: Positive for CH₃CO– groups and CH₃CH(OH)– groups.

formulas.name: Other key tests
formulas.formula: 2,4-DNPH: orange precipitate (any C=O of aldehyde/ketone); neutral FeCl₃: violet (phenol); Lucas (ZnCl₂/HCl): cloudiness fast for 3°, slower for 2°, none quickly for 1° alcohol
formulas.note: Know reagent, observation and the group detected.

shortcuts.name: Iodoform pattern spotting
shortcuts.rule: Look for CH₃ attached to C=O or to CH(OH). Any such compound is positive.
shortcuts.example: Positive: ethanol (the only positive primary alcohol), ethanal (the only positive aldehyde), propanone, butan-2-ol. Negative: methanol, propan-1-ol, pentan-3-one.

shortcuts.name: Three-reagent elimination grid
shortcuts.rule: NaHCO₃ fizz means COOH. Dissolves in NaOH but no NaHCO₃ fizz means phenol. Fizzes only with Na means alcohol. No reaction with Na means ether, ester or ketone.
shortcuts.example: An unknown fizzes with Na, does not dissolve in NaOH and does not react with NaHCO₃: it is an alcohol.

shortcuts.name: Hydrogen from –OH count
shortcuts.rule: Each –OH group gives ½ H₂ with Na; 1 mol of gas = 22.4 dm³ at STP.
shortcuts.example: 1 mol ethane-1,2-diol (2 OH) gives 1 mol H₂ = 22.4 dm³. 1 mol glycerol (3 OH) gives 1.5 mol = 33.6 dm³.

shortcuts.name: Ester molar mass
shortcuts.rule: Mr(ester) = Mr(acid) + Mr(alcohol) − 18.
shortcuts.example: Ethyl ethanoate: 60 + 46 − 18 = 88. Methyl methanoate: 46 + 32 − 18 = 60.

shortcuts.name: Hydrolysis back-naming
shortcuts.rule: Cut the ester name in two: the first word is the alcohol (-yl becomes -anol), the second the acid (-oate becomes -oic acid).
shortcuts.example: Methyl propanoate hydrolyses to methanol + propanoic acid. Pentyl ethanoate (banana smell) gives pentan-1-ol + ethanoic acid.

shortcuts.name: Oxidation by counting H on the C–OH carbon
shortcuts.rule: 2 H on that carbon: can go to aldehyde, then acid. 1 H: to ketone. 0 H: no oxidation, dichromate stays orange.
shortcuts.example: 2-methylpropan-2-ol (no H on the C–OH carbon) leaves K₂Cr₂O₇ orange. Propan-2-ol (1 H) gives propanone.

traps: Saying ketones give a silver mirror. Only aldehydes (and methanoic acid) reduce Tollens' reagent; both aldehydes and ketones give 2,4-DNPH.
Forgetting that the aldehyde must be distilled off as it forms. Heating under reflux oxidises it all the way to the acid.
Calling conc H₂SO₄ a reactant in esterification. It is a catalyst (and absorbs water to shift the equilibrium).
Mixing up aqueous KOH (substitution, gives alcohol) and ethanolic KOH (elimination, gives alkene).
Writing the ester name backwards: CH₃COOCH₃ is methyl ethanoate, not ethyl methanoate.
nsmqTips: Test questions are answered as reagent + observation + inference, e.g. 'warm with Tollens': silver mirror, so aldehyde'. Give all three in one breath.
For 'which of these gives a yellow precipitate with I₂/NaOH?' scan only for CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)–. Elimination is faster than drawing every structure.
Know smells of esters for riddles: pentyl ethanoate (banana), octyl ethanoate (orange), methyl salicylate (wintergreen), ethyl butanoate (pineapple).

topics.summary: Addition and condensation polymers, natural macromolecules (carbohydrates, proteins, fats), soaps and detergents, and the petrochemical industry. NSMQ asks students to identify monomers, classify polymerisation types, do repeat-unit calculations and recall food tests.
keyIdeas: Addition polymerisation joins unsaturated monomers (C=C) with no by-product. Condensation polymerisation joins bifunctional monomers with loss of a small molecule (usually H₂O or HCl).
Polyamides (nylon, proteins) contain –CO–NH– links. Polyesters (Terylene/PET, Dacron) contain –CO–O– links. These can be hydrolysed and are more biodegradable than addition polymers.
Thermoplastics (polyethene, PVC) soften on heating and can be remoulded. Thermosets (Bakelite, melamine) are cross-linked and char instead of melting.
Carbohydrates are Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose) and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose).
Proteins are polymers of α-amino acids (H₂N–CHR–COOH) linked by peptide bonds. Amino acids are amphoteric and exist as zwitterions.
Fats and oils are triesters of glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) with fatty acids. Oils are unsaturated (liquid); fats are mostly saturated (solid).
Soaps are sodium/potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids and form scum with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ in hard water. Soapless detergents (alkylbenzene sulphonates) do not.
Petrochemicals: fractional distillation of crude oil (Tema Oil Refinery in Ghana), cracking and reforming provide ethene, propene and aromatics as polymer feedstocks.

formulas.name: Polyethene
formulas.note: Addition polymer. LDPE (branched) or HDPE (Ziegler–Natta catalyst, linear).

formulas.name: Common addition monomers
formulas.formula: PVC: CH₂=CHCl (chloroethene); PTFE: CF₂=CF₂; polystyrene: CH₂=CHC₆H₅ (phenylethene); polypropene: CH₂=CHCH₃; Perspex: CH₂=C(CH₃)COOCH₃
formulas.note: Repeat unit = monomer with C=C opened to C–C.

formulas.name: Nylon-6,6
formulas.note: Hexane-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid. Condensation; amide links.

formulas.name: Terylene (PET)
formulas.note: Condensation; ester links. Used for fabrics and bottles.

formulas.name: Natural rubber
formulas.note: Vulcanisation with sulphur forms S–S cross-links, which make it harder and more elastic.

formulas.name: Disaccharide hydrolysis
formulas.note: Sucrose → glucose + fructose; maltose → 2 glucose; lactose → glucose + galactose.

formulas.name: Polysaccharides
formulas.formula: Starch and glycogen: α-glucose polymers; cellulose: β-glucose polymer (β-1,4 links)
formulas.note: Humans cannot digest cellulose (no cellulase).

formulas.name: Saponification of fat
formulas.note: Boil fat or oil with NaOH, then salt out the soap with NaCl.

formulas.name: Degree of polymerisation
formulas.note: For addition polymers, Mr(repeat unit) = Mr(monomer).

formulas.name: Food tests
formulas.formula: Starch: iodine, blue-black; reducing sugar: Benedict's/Fehling's, brick-red; protein: biuret (NaOH + CuSO₄), violet; fat: ethanol emulsion, cloudy white (or translucent grease spot)
formulas.note: Sucrose is non-reducing: boil with dilute HCl, neutralise, then do Benedict's.

formulas.name: Hardening of oils
formulas.note: Converts vegetable oil to margarine.

shortcuts.name: Repeat unit by 'open the double bond'
shortcuts.rule: Replace C=C by C–C, put the side groups on the chain, and add brackets with n. Mr(repeat unit) = Mr(monomer).
shortcuts.example: Propene CH₂=CHCH₃ gives –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]ₙ–, repeat Mr = 42. A polypropene of Mr 84 000 has n = 2000.

shortcuts.name: Degree of polymerisation by easy division
shortcuts.rule: Divide by the monomer Mr using round numbers: ethene 28, chloroethene 62.5, styrene 104, tetrafluoroethene 100.
shortcuts.example: Polyethene of Mr 28 000 gives n = 1000. PVC of Mr 125 000 gives n = 125 000/62.5 = 2000. PTFE of Mr 50 000 gives n = 500.

shortcuts.name: (n − 1) water rule
shortcuts.rule: Linking n monomer units in a chain by condensation releases (n − 1) H₂O. Mass of chain = sum of monomers − 18(n − 1).
shortcuts.example: Tripeptide from 3 glycine (Mr 75): 3×75 − 2×18 = 225 − 36 = 189. Sucrose: 180 + 180 − 18 = 342.

shortcuts.name: Nylon-x,y code
shortcuts.rule: x = number of C atoms in the diamine, y = number of C atoms in the diacid.
shortcuts.example: Nylon-6,10 is made from hexane-1,6-diamine (6 C) and decanedioic acid (10 C).

shortcuts.name: Peptide sequence count
shortcuts.rule: With n different amino acids each used once, the number of linear sequences is n!.
shortcuts.example: Gly, Ala, Val each once: 3! = 6 tripeptides. Gly and Ala each once: 2 dipeptides (Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly).

shortcuts.name: Addition or condensation at a glance
shortcuts.rule: Monomer has C=C: addition. Two different functional groups on the monomers (–OH, –COOH, –NH₂, –COCl): condensation.
shortcuts.example: Tetrafluoroethene gives PTFE by addition. Ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid gives PET by condensation.

traps: Calling sucrose a reducing sugar. It is non-reducing; glucose, fructose, maltose and lactose are reducing.
Saying addition polymerisation releases water. It releases nothing, so the mass of polymer equals the mass of monomer used.
Thinking soaps work well in hard water. They form insoluble scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺; soapless detergents do not.
Confusing starch and cellulose. Both are glucose polymers, but starch is α-linked (digestible) and cellulose β-linked (indigestible to humans).
Naming the nylon-6,6 diacid as hexanoic acid. It is hexanedioic acid (two COOH groups).
nsmqTips: 'Name the monomer of X' questions are common. Have the five addition polymers and their monomers as a fixed list.
Food-test riddles: listen for the colour word. Blue-black means starch, brick-red means reducing sugar, violet/purple means protein, grease spot means fat.
Degree-of-polymerisation numbers are chosen to divide neatly. If your answer is not a round number, recheck the monomer Mr.

topics.summary: How organic reactions happen step by step, shown with curly arrows: free-radical, nucleophilic substitution (SN1, SN2), elimination, electrophilic addition and substitution, and nucleophilic addition. It also covers how IR, NMR, mass spectrometry and UV–visible spectroscopy identify structures. NSMQ uses the basic mechanism ideas, and first-year university courses add rate laws, stereochemistry and spectral interpretation.
keyIdeas: Homolytic fission gives radicals (one electron each); heterolytic fission gives ions. A curly arrow shows the movement of an electron pair, from electron-rich to electron-poor.
Nucleophiles donate an electron pair (OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O); electrophiles accept one (H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br^δ+, carbocations).
SN2: one step, backside attack, rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion of configuration. Favoured by methyl and primary substrates and polar aprotic solvents.
SN1: two steps through a carbocation, rate = k[RX], racemisation. Favoured by tertiary substrates and polar protic solvents.
Carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl (alkyl groups donate electron density by induction and hyperconjugation). This explains Markovnikov addition and SN1 preference.
Electrophilic aromatic substitution: the electrophile attacks the π ring to give an arenium (Wheland) intermediate, then H⁺ is lost so aromaticity is restored.
Carbonyls undergo nucleophilic addition (e.g. HCN/CN⁻ gives a cyanohydrin), because the C of C=O is δ+.

IR identifies functional groups by bond vibrations. ¹H NMR gives H environments (number of signals), their type (chemical shift), relative numbers (integration) and neighbours (splitting). MS gives Mr and fragments.

formulas.name: Rate laws
formulas.formula: SN2: rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]; SN1: rate = k[RX]
formulas.note: Second order vs first order overall. E2 and E1 follow the same pattern.

formulas.name: Nitronium ion formation
formulas.note: NO₂⁺ is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene.

formulas.name: Halogen carrier
formulas.note: Generates the electrophile for aromatic bromination. AlCl₃ plays the same role in Friedel–Crafts reactions.

formulas.name: Beer–Lambert law
formulas.note: A = absorbance (no unit), ε = molar absorptivity (dm³ mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹), c in mol dm⁻³, l = path length in cm.

formulas.name: Photon energy and wavenumber
formulas.formula: E = hν = hc/λ = hcν̃, with ν̃ = 1/λ
formulas.note: IR uses wavenumber in cm⁻¹. Higher wavenumber means a stiffer bond or lighter atoms.

formulas.name: Key IR absorptions (cm⁻¹)
formulas.note: The region below 1500 cm⁻¹ is the fingerprint region.

formulas.name: ¹H NMR chemical shifts (δ, ppm)
formulas.note: Relative to TMS (δ = 0). Electronegative neighbours shift signals downfield (higher δ).

formulas.name: n + 1 rule
formulas.formula: Signal splits into n + 1 peaks, where n = equivalent H on adjacent carbons
formulas.note: Peak intensities follow Pascal's triangle: doublet 1:1, triplet 1:2:1, quartet 1:3:3:1.

formulas.name: Carbon count from M+1 peak
formulas.note: ¹³C is about 1.1% of natural carbon.

formulas.name: Halogen isotope patterns
formulas.formula: One Cl: M : M+2 = 3 : 1; one Br: M : M+2 = 1 : 1
formulas.note: From ³⁵Cl:³⁷Cl ≈ 3:1 and ⁷⁹Br:⁸¹Br ≈ 1:1.

formulas.name: Common MS fragments (m/z)
formulas.formula: 15 CH₃⁺; 29 C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺; 43 CH₃CO⁺ or C₃H₇⁺; 77 C₆H₅⁺; 91 C₇H₇⁺
formulas.note: The base peak is the tallest peak; the molecular ion is the highest-m/z peak (except isotope peaks).

shortcuts.name: Carbon count by dividing by 1.1
shortcuts.rule: M+1 percentage ÷ 1.1 = number of carbons.
shortcuts.example: M+1 is 4.4% of M: 4.4/1.1 = 4 carbons. M+1 is 6.6%: 6 carbons.

shortcuts.name: Halogen fingerprints
shortcuts.rule: M, M+2 heights: 3:1 means one Cl; 1:1 means one Br; 9:6:1 (M, M+2, M+4) means two Cl; 1:2:1 means two Br.
shortcuts.example: Peaks at m/z 78 and 80 in 3:1 ratio: one Cl. C₃H₇Cl has Mr 78 (with ³⁵Cl), so the compound is a chloropropane.

shortcuts.name: Ethyl and isopropyl signatures
shortcuts.rule: Triplet (3H) + quartet (2H) means an ethyl group. Doublet (6H) + septet (1H) means an isopropyl group.
shortcuts.example: Ethanol: CH₃ triplet, CH₂ quartet, OH singlet (3 signals, ratio 3:2:1).

shortcuts.name: Count NMR signals by symmetry
shortcuts.rule: Group H atoms that can be swapped by symmetry; each group is one signal.
shortcuts.example: Propanone: 1 signal. Propan-2-ol: 3 (2 equivalent CH₃, CH, OH). Propan-1-ol: 4 (CH₃, CH₂, CH₂O, OH). Benzene: 1.

shortcuts.name: Nitrogen rule
shortcuts.rule: An odd molecular-ion m/z means an odd number of N atoms (for C, H, O, N, halogen compounds).
shortcuts.example: M⁺ at m/z 59 suggests one N: C₃H₉N (36 + 9 + 14 = 59), e.g. propylamine. M⁺ at 60 with no N could be propanol or ethanoic acid.

shortcuts.name: Mechanism from rate data
shortcuts.rule: If doubling [Nu⁻] doubles the rate, it is SN2. If the rate does not change, it is SN1.
shortcuts.example: (CH₃)₃CBr hydrolysis: doubling [OH⁻] leaves the rate unchanged, so SN1 through the stable tertiary carbocation.

traps: Drawing a curly arrow from an atom's nucleus or from a positive centre. Arrows start at a lone pair or a bond, never at a positive charge.
Saying SN1 at a chiral centre gives inversion. SN2 gives inversion; SN1 gives (mostly) racemisation through a planar carbocation.
Taking the base peak to be the molecular ion. M⁺ is the highest-m/z (non-isotope) peak and may be small.
Splitting NMR signals by the O–H proton or by equivalent protons. Under normal conditions OH is a singlet, and equivalent H do not split each other.
Reading any absorption near 3300 cm⁻¹ as an alcohol. Check for the very broad acid O–H (2500–3300) paired with C=O at about 1710.
nsmqTips: Mechanism questions in NSMQ are usually naming: 'free-radical substitution', 'electrophilic addition', 'nucleophilic substitution'. Match reactant type to mechanism: alkane + UV gives radical; alkene gives electrophilic addition; haloalkane + OH⁻ gives nucleophilic substitution; benzene gives electrophilic substitution.
For spectra, read the IR for the functional group first, then use MS for Mr, then NMR for the skeleton. That order narrows choices fastest.
Remember the electrophile names: NO₂⁺ nitronium, CH₃CO⁺ acylium, Br⁺ via FeBr₃.

topics.summary: Radioactivity (α, β and γ decay, half-life, nuclear equations, fission and fusion) and the chemistry of the environment: air pollution, acid rain, the greenhouse effect, ozone depletion and water quality. NSMQ asks quick half-life arithmetic, decay-series counting and the chemistry behind current environmental issues such as galamsey mercury pollution.
keyIdeas: α particle = ⁴₂He nucleus (A −4, Z −2). β⁻ particle = electron from the nucleus as n → p (A same, Z +1). γ = high-energy photon (no change in A or Z).
Penetration: α is stopped by paper, β by a few mm of aluminium, γ is only reduced by thick lead or concrete. Ionising power is the reverse order.
Half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay. It is constant for a nuclide and does not depend on temperature, pressure, amount or chemical form.

Fission splits heavy nuclei (²³⁵U) with release of neutrons and energy (chain reaction); fusion joins light nuclei (H isotopes) and powers the Sun. Both release energy from mass defect. Ghana's research reactor GHARR-1 is at Kwabenya.
Uses: ¹⁴C dating, ⁶⁰Co radiotherapy and sterilisation, ¹³¹I thyroid treatment, ²⁴¹Am smoke detectors, tracers.
Acid rain comes from SO₂ (burning fossil fuels, smelting) and NOx (vehicle engines). It corrodes metals and limestone, harms plants and acidifies lakes.
Stratospheric ozone absorbs UV and is destroyed catalytically by Cl radicals from CFCs. The greenhouse effect (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O, CFCs absorbing IR) is a different problem.
Water pollutants include heavy metals (Hg from galamsey gold amalgamation, Pb, Cd), excess nitrates and phosphates (eutrophication) and organic waste (raises BOD).

formulas.name: Alpha decay
formulas.note: Mass number falls by 4, atomic number by 2.

formulas.name: Beta-minus decay
formulas.note: A neutron becomes a proton. β⁺ (positron) decay lowers Z by 1 instead.

formulas.name: Radioactive decay law
formulas.note: N = nuclei (or mass, or activity) remaining after time t.

formulas.name: Decay constant and activity
formulas.formula: λ = ln2 / t½ ≈ 0.693 / t½; A = λN
formulas.note: A in becquerels (Bq = decays per second) when λ is in s⁻¹.

formulas.name: Counting α and β in a series
formulas.formula: Number of α = ΔA / 4; number of β⁻ = 2(number of α) − ΔZ
formulas.note: ΔA and ΔZ are the drops in mass and atomic number from parent to final product.

formulas.name: Mass–energy
formulas.note: Δm = mass defect = (mass of separate nucleons) − (mass of nucleus).

formulas.name: Fission example
formulas.note: The released neutrons sustain the chain reaction. Moderators (graphite, water) slow neutrons; control rods (B, Cd) absorb them.

formulas.name: Acid rain chemistry
formulas.note: Unpolluted rain has pH ≈ 5.6 from dissolved CO₂; acid rain is below that.

formulas.name: Ozone depletion by CFCs
formulas.formula: CFCl₃ → CFCl₂• + Cl• (UV); Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂
formulas.note: Cl• is regenerated, so one Cl atom can destroy thousands of O₃ molecules.

formulas.name: Water hardness
formulas.formula: Temporary: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ (boiling); permanent: CaSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃ + Na₂SO₄
formulas.note: Temporary hardness is removed by boiling; permanent needs washing soda, ion exchange or distillation.

formulas.name: Carbon-14 half-life
formulas.note: Used to date once-living material up to about 50 000 years old.

shortcuts.name: α first, then β
shortcuts.rule: Get α from the drop in A (÷ 4), see how far Z would fall, and make up the difference with β⁻.
shortcuts.example: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb: ΔA = 32 gives 8α, which would take Z to 92 − 16 = 76. Actual Z is 82, so 6β⁻ (check: 2×8 − 10 = 6).

shortcuts.name: Halving chain
shortcuts.rule: Count half-lives n = t/t½; remaining = start ÷ 2ⁿ; decayed fraction = 1 − 1/2ⁿ.
shortcuts.example: 80 g with t½ = 5 days, after 20 days: n = 4, so 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 g left; 15/16 has decayed.

shortcuts.name: Fraction to age
shortcuts.rule: Recognise 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 as 1, 2, 3, 4 half-lives.
shortcuts.example: Wood with 25% of the original ¹⁴C: 2 half-lives = 2 × 5730 = 11 460 years. With 12.5% left: 3 half-lives = 17 190 years.

shortcuts.name: Balance tops and bottoms
shortcuts.rule: Sum of mass numbers and sum of atomic numbers must match on both sides. Find the missing particle by subtraction.
shortcuts.example: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + x n: 236 = 141 + 92 + x, so x = 3. Check Z: 92 = 56 + 36.

shortcuts.name: Mass defect to MeV
shortcuts.rule: Multiply the mass defect in u by about 930 (931.5).
shortcuts.example: Mass defect 0.030 u gives 0.030 × 931.5 ≈ 28 MeV, which is about the binding energy of ⁴He.

shortcuts.name: Which decay? Use the stability belt
shortcuts.rule: Too many neutrons (above the belt): β⁻. Too few neutrons: β⁺ or electron capture. Z > 83: usually α.
shortcuts.example: ¹⁴C (8 n, 6 p) is neutron-rich, so it decays by β⁻ to ¹⁴N. ²²⁶Ra (Z = 88) decays by α to ²²²Rn.

traps: Thinking heating or compressing a sample changes its half-life. Radioactive decay is unaffected by physical and chemical conditions.
Saying the β⁻ electron comes from the electron shells. It is created in the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton.
Treating all rain below pH 7 as acid rain. Normal rain is about pH 5.6 because of dissolved CO₂.
Confusing ozone depletion (CFCs, UV getting through) with global warming (greenhouse gases trapping IR), or calling ground-level ozone protective (it is a pollutant).
Forgetting that γ emission changes neither mass number nor atomic number. It often follows α or β decay.
nsmqTips: Half-life questions are built for mental halving. Count the halvings on your fingers and do not reach for logarithms unless t/t½ is not a whole number.
Decay-series questions ('how many α and β particles?') come up often. Answer α from ΔA/4 first; the β count follows in one subtraction.
Environmental riddles often use Ghanaian context: galamsey means mercury (Hg) pollution and turbid rivers; burning e-waste at Agbogbloshie means lead and dioxin pollution.

topics.summary: Safe and accurate laboratory technique (titration, separation methods, handling apparatus), plus systematic tests to identify cations, anions and gases. The WASSCE practical and NSMQ both reward knowing exact reagents, observations and colours.
keyIdeas: Rinse the burette with the solution it will hold and the pipette with the solution it will deliver. Rinse the conical flask with distilled water only.

Read the burette at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus (top of the meniscus for dark solutions such as KMnO₄). Record readings to 2 decimal places (±0.05 cm³). Concordant titres agree within about 0.10 cm³.
Choose the indicator by the strength of the acid and base. Strong acid–weak base: methyl orange. Weak acid–strong base: phenolphthalein. Weak–weak: no simple indicator works.

Separation: filtration (insoluble solid), evaporation/crystallisation (dissolved solid), simple distillation (solvent from solution), fractional distillation (miscible liquids), separating funnel (immiscible liquids), sublimation (NH₄Cl, I₂), chromatography (dyes, pigments).
Cations are identified by the colour of their hydroxide precipitates with NaOH(aq) and NH₃(aq), and whether the precipitate dissolves in excess. Flame tests give metal-ion colours.
Anions: halides with acidified AgNO₃, sulphate with acidified BaCl₂, carbonate with dilute acid (CO₂), nitrate with the brown-ring test or Devarda's alloy.
Safety: add acid to water, never water to concentrated acid. Use a fume cupboard for toxic gases (Cl₂, SO₂, NO₂, H₂S). Point test tubes away from people when heating.

formulas.name: Titration relation
formulas.note: nₐ and n_b are the stoichiometric coefficients of acid and base in the balanced equation.

formulas.name: Mass concentration
formulas.note: M = molar mass in g mol⁻¹.

formulas.name: Percentage error
formulas.note: A titre from two burette readings has an uncertainty of ±0.10 cm³.

formulas.name: Rf value
formulas.formula: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front
formulas.note: Always between 0 and 1; measured from the baseline.

formulas.name: Hydroxide precipitates with NaOH(aq)
formulas.formula: Cu²⁺ blue; Fe²⁺ dirty green (browns in air); Fe³⁺ reddish-brown; Zn²⁺, Al³⁺, Pb²⁺ white, soluble in excess; Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ white, insoluble in excess; NH₄⁺ no precipitate, NH₃ on warming
formulas.note: Add NaOH dropwise, then in excess.

formulas.name: Precipitates with NH₃(aq)
formulas.formula: Cu²⁺ pale blue precipitate, dissolves in excess to deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺; Zn²⁺ white, dissolves in excess ([Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺); Al³⁺ and Pb²⁺ white, insoluble in excess
formulas.note: The key way to tell Zn²⁺ from Al³⁺ and Pb²⁺.

formulas.name: Halide test
formulas.note: Acidify with dilute HNO₃ first. AgCl dissolves in dilute NH₃, AgBr in concentrated NH₃, AgI in neither.

formulas.name: Sulphate test
formulas.formula: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ (white, insoluble in dilute HCl)
formulas.note: Acidify with dilute HCl or HNO₃ first to remove carbonate and sulphite.

formulas.name: Nitrate tests
formulas.formula: Brown ring (FeSO₄ + conc H₂SO₄ down the side); or warm with NaOH + Devarda's alloy (Al) to give NH₃
formulas.note: The brown ring is [Fe(H₂O)₅NO]²⁺ at the junction of the layers.

formulas.name: Flame colours
formulas.formula: Li crimson; Na golden yellow; K lilac; Ca brick red; Sr crimson red; Ba apple green; Cu blue-green
formulas.note: Use a clean nichrome or platinum wire dipped in conc HCl.

formulas.name: Specific iron tests
formulas.formula: Fe³⁺ + KSCN: blood-red; Fe²⁺ + K₃[Fe(CN)₆]: dark blue (Turnbull's blue)
formulas.note: Confirmatory tests beyond NaOH.

shortcuts.name: ZAP the amphoterics
shortcuts.rule: Zn, Al and Pb hydroxides dissolve in excess NaOH. Then use NH₃: only Zn's precipitate dissolves in excess NH₃.
shortcuts.example: A white precipitate with NaOH dissolves in excess NaOH, and with NH₃ the white precipitate also dissolves in excess: Zn²⁺.

shortcuts.name: One-line titration arithmetic
shortcuts.rule: Cₐ = C_b × V_b × nₐ / (n_b × Vₐ). Keep volumes in cm³ because they cancel.
shortcuts.example: 20.0 cm³ H₂SO₄ neutralises 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH (ratio 1:2): Cₐ = 0.100 × 25.0 × 1 / (2 × 20.0) = 2.5/40 = 0.0625 mol dm⁻³.

shortcuts.name: Indicator follows the strong partner
shortcuts.rule: Phenolphthalein (alkaline range) when the base is strong; methyl orange (acidic range) when the acid is strong; either when both are strong.
shortcuts.example: Ethanoic acid vs NaOH: phenolphthalein. HCl vs NH₃(aq): methyl orange. HCl vs NaOH: either.

shortcuts.name: Silver halide colour ladder
shortcuts.rule: Down Group 17 the precipitate darkens (white, cream, yellow) and becomes less soluble in NH₃ (dilute, concentrated, insoluble).
shortcuts.example: A cream precipitate that dissolves only in concentrated NH₃ means Br⁻.

shortcuts.name: Rf in your head
shortcuts.rule: Rf = spot ÷ front. Turn it into a fraction you know.
shortcuts.example: Spot at 3.0 cm, front at 7.5 cm: 3.0/7.5 = 2/5 = 0.40. A spot with Rf 0.6 and front 8.0 cm sits at 4.8 cm.

shortcuts.name: Iron by colour
shortcuts.rule: Fe²⁺ is green (fresh); Fe³⁺ is rust-coloured. A green precipitate that browns on standing shows Fe²⁺ oxidising to Fe³⁺.
shortcuts.example: NaOH gives a dirty green precipitate turning brown at the surface: Fe²⁺. An immediate reddish-brown precipitate: Fe³⁺.

traps: Acidifying with HCl before the AgNO₃ halide test: it adds Cl⁻ and always gives a white precipitate. Use dilute HNO₃.
Adding an indicator to KMnO₄ titrations. KMnO₄ is self-indicating (colourless to permanent pale pink). Acidify with dilute H₂SO₄, not HCl, which KMnO₄ oxidises.
Rinsing the conical flask with the solution to be titrated. This adds extra moles; rinse it with distilled water only.
Mixing up Pb²⁺ and Al³⁺. Both give white precipitates soluble in excess NaOH and insoluble in excess NH₃; distinguish with KI (yellow PbI₂) or dilute HCl (white PbCl₂).
Reading the burette from above or below eye level (parallax), or recording to only one decimal place.
nsmqTips: Qualitative-analysis riddles give a chain of observations. Lock the cation from NaOH/NH₃ behaviour, then the anion from the silver or barium test, and name the salt.
Flame-test colour questions are rapid-fire. Say 'lilac' for K and 'apple green' for Ba exactly; vague colours may not be accepted.
For titration calculations, write the mole ratio first and use the one-line formula. NSMQ numbers are chosen to give clean decimals like 0.0625 or 0.125.
